title: question buttons: tapped answer never reaches the agent (CC >=2.1.198 requires hookEventName); multi-question ends on an extra manual Enter
body:
## What
Bug 1: formatAgentHookOutput (claude+question) emits hookSpecificOutput WITHOUT the required hookEventName:'PreToolUse'. Claude Code >=2.1.198 validates hook JSON output and discards the whole output without it (dedicated parser error: hookSpecificOutput is missing required field hookEventName) — the Telegram card reads 'answered: …' while the agent falls back to the local dialog. Incident proof: daemon log ask-answered key=claude-rkq4bd messageId=5740 delivered down the LIVE socket (questions.json delivery:'socket') one minute before the complaint. Secondary: the rebuilt updatedInput is lossy (drops option preview, may drop required description) while 2.1.198 schema-validates updatedInput wholesale. Bug 2: hook-normalize bails to the local UI for questions.length !== 1, so a 2-4-question AskUserQuestion is never forwarded and the local multi-question dialog ends on an extra final Enter; the 2.1.198 schema supports 1-4 questions + an answers record and call() returns input.answers directly.

## Why (motivation)
The q->buttons flow is the CTO's primary way to answer fleet questions from his phone; it silently died on a Claude Code contract drift the spec itself predicted (canary was deferred).

## User impact
Every question forwarded to Telegram is lost: the CTO taps an answer, the card claims success, the agent stalls on a local dialog nobody watches — hours of fleet stall per missed question.

## Cost of inaction
All tg question buttons keep lying about delivery; multi-question flows keep requiring manual terminal Enter presses, defeating remote operation.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A tap on a live claude question completes AskUserQuestion: integration test asserts the emitted envelope carries hookEventName:'PreToolUse' and echoes the original tool_input + answers
- [ ] A 2-question AskUserQuestion forwards as two sequential cards and after the LAST tap the ask client emits ONE combined reply with both answers (e2e test against the fake local Telegram server, never a real chat)

title: Answered unscoped blocker never flushes deferred backlog; ✍️ never flips to 👀 (tg#5855)
body:
## What is wrong

Reported by Alex (tg#5855, verbatim): «tg ставит ✍️ реакцию но после того как блокер снят не меняет на глазки и видимо и не отправляет агенту».

Two independent defects in the defer-while-waiting pipeline:

1. **Delivery (critical).** `answer-question` flushes the defer queue only via `pending.req.paneId`. A permission/question forwarded by a hook that ran **without TMUX_PANE** (the common Claude Code case) is UNSCOPED — `paneId === undefined` — yet that same unscoped entry defers inbound for EVERY pane (fail-closed, tg#30). Its answer therefore flushes **nothing**: queued messages sit in `DeferQueues` indefinitely and never reach the agent.
2. **Receipt.** Deferred items carry only the wrapped text — no source `message_id` — so nothing can ever flip the ✍️ "queued" reaction to 👀 when the item lands (this is broken even on the scoped path).

## Evidence

Regression test red on the pre-fix daemon (integration, fake Bot API + fake tmux, no real chat):
`tests/ctl-defer-integration.test.ts` → "tg#5855: answering an UNSCOPED permission flushes the deferred backlog and flips its ✍️ to 👀" fails at the delivery assertion (`injected()` never contains the deferred text) against origin/main's `tg-ctl`.

## User impact

Messages Alex sends while an agent is blocked on a permission look "noted" (✍️) but are silently never delivered after he answers the blocker — lost instructions, and the reaction lies about the state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Answering an unscoped permission/question flushes every pane's deferred backlog (integration test, red→green proven).
- [ ] A flushed deferred message's reaction flips ✍️ → 👀 (scoped and unscoped paths).
- [ ] A dead-lettered (never delivered) message does NOT keep ✍️ — reaction cleared, user notice already exists.
- [ ] Full suite green.

title: Reply quote-anchor should carry the original message's tg#<id>
body:
## What
When Alex replies/quotes a message in Telegram, the daemon injects a one-line
quote anchor (`buildReplyAnchor`, `features/tg-ctl/updates.ts`) identifying
what he answered — but the anchor never carried the replied-to message's own
Telegram id, only a truncated (~60 char) text preview.

Separately, the reply's OWN id is already surfaced via the `{id}` substitution
in `wrapInbound` (tg#28) — but that's the id of Alex's new message, not the
original one he's answering.

## Why
Alex (tg#5978): "Сделай чтобы при цитировании и реплаях пользователем в тг
указывался tg#NNN сообщения агента, чтобы он мог через tg replies прочитать
его, если забыл" — an agent whose context has compacted/forgotten the
original message has no way to recover it beyond the truncated preview. It
needs the original message's own tg#<id> so it can look the full text back up
via `tg replies` (e.g. `tg replies agent --all-sessions --json` filtered by
id) instead of guessing.

## Acceptance
- The quote anchor built by `buildReplyAnchor`/`buildReplyInject` renders
  `reply_to_message.message_id` as `tg#<id>` (same convention as tg#28),
  alongside the existing `[date time] head…` preview.
- Applies uniformly to text replies, voice-note replies, and prose replies

title: tg replies: multi-id sends (split/album) show duplicate lines in list/find
body:
## Context

PR #131 added a `tg#<id>` anchor to reply-quotes so an agent can recover the
original message verbatim via `tg replies --json | select(.id == <tg#>)`.
A review thread on that PR (chatgpt-codex-connector, P2) pointed out that
`recordOutboundHistory` only ever wrote ONE `agent` history record keyed to
`firstOutboundId`, while a >4096-char split or a media-group album emits
SEVERAL Telegram `message_id`s for one logical send — so a reply anchored to
a non-first id had no matching history record and the recall path silently
returned nothing.

That was fixed in the same PR: `buildOutboundHistoryRecords`
(`features/replies/outbound.ts`) now writes one history record per outbound
`message_id` (same text, same ts/pane), so recall-by-id works for every
anchored id.

## The follow-up gap (not fixed in #131 — deliberately deferred)

A second-pass `review diff` on that fix flagged a real side effect: writing
one row per id means `features/replies/select.ts` (`selectHistory`,
`formatLines`) — used by `tg replies agent` / `tg replies find` — now treats
every one of those rows as a separate, user-visible list entry. A 10-photo
album or a 3-chunk long-report split will show up as 10 or 3 *duplicate*
`[time] #id text` lines instead of one, and will consume more of the default
`-n 20` window than before, pushing older distinct messages out of view
sooner.

## Why deferred

Fixing recall-by-id was the narrow, blocking ask from the PR #131 review
thread. Fixing the list/find duplication requires an actual design decision
(a reader-side grouping/alias strategy, or a different schema that keeps
per-id lookup while collapsing list/find rendering back to one logical
line per send) — that's bigger than a drive-by fix and deserves its own
pass + tests rather than being rushed into the id-recall fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `tg replies agent` / `tg replies find` render ONE line per logical
      outbound send, even when that send produced multiple Telegram
      `message_id`s (split or album), while `tg replies --json | select(.id
      == <tg#>)` still resolves for ANY of those ids.
- [ ] A `runReplies` roundtrip test covers a multi-id send end-to-end: write
      history for a 3-chunk split (or N-photo album), then assert `list`
      shows exactly one line and `--json` selection succeeds for a non-first
      id.

## Pointers

- `features/replies/outbound.ts` — `buildOutboundHistoryRecords` (the fix
  that introduced the duplicate rows as a side effect)
- `features/replies/select.ts:75` (`selectHistory`) and `:123`
  (`formatLines`) — where every row is currently rendered as its own line
- `tests/replies-roundtrip.test.ts` — existing roundtrip test pattern to
  extend

title: tg replies history.jsonl: outbound writer has no RMW lock (unlike routes.json)
body:
## Context

`recordOutboundHistory` in `tg` (the CLI entrypoint) does a plain
read-modify-write on the history log: `readFileSync` -> `appendRecordsToBlob`
-> `writeFileSync`, with NO cross-process lock. This is pre-existing (predates
PR #131) and shared with the `tg-ctl` daemon's inbound poll-loop writer.

Contrast with `features/tg-ctl/routes.ts`, which has a real cross-process
mutex (`withRoutesLock` / `fsRoutesLockIo`, an O_EXCL lockfile with
PID-liveness-based staleness) specifically because two `tg` sends racing an
unlocked RMW would last-writer-wins-clobber each other's entries.

## Why this matters more after #131

PR #131's fix (`buildOutboundHistoryRecords`) made a single `tg` invocation
write MULTIPLE history records per send (one per outbound Telegram
message_id — a >4096 split or a media-group album can be 3-10+ ids) instead
of one. This doesn't introduce the missing-lock issue, but it does widen the
unlocked read-modify-write window per invocation (more writes = more time
with the file open for RMW), so the pre-existing lost-update risk under
concurrent `tg` sends from multiple panes/agents is somewhat amplified.

## What's NOT at risk

`buildOutboundHistoryRecords` already de-dupes ids WITHIN one call (protects
against a single call's retry double-reporting an id), and `routes.json`
itself is unaffected (it already has the lock). This issue is specifically
about `history.jsonl`'s RMW.

## Suggested fix

Either:
1. Reuse the same `withRoutesLock`/`fsRoutesLockIo` machinery
   (`features/tg-ctl/routes.ts`) for the history file's RMW (a second
   lockfile, or a shared lock keyed by path), matching `routes.ts`'s
   already-proven pattern, or
2. Accept the risk as low-severity (history is a best-effort recall aid, not
   a source of truth — a lost update just means one send's history record(s)
   don't get appended, not corruption) and document it explicitly as a known
   trade-off in the file header comment.

## Pointers

- `tg` — `recordOutboundHistory` (the outbound writer, unlocked)
- the `tg-ctl` daemon's inbound poll-loop writer (also unlocked, same file)
- `features/tg-ctl/routes.ts` — `withRoutesLock` / `fsRoutesLockIo`, the
  existing proven lock pattern to reuse or mirror

title: --title should refuse a tg#<id> reference
body:
## What
tg-cli's --title flag sets the one-line header on a message (the window-name line). Unlike the message body/caption, nothing downstream ever linkifies a title -- the msgref linkifier only runs on the body. So a tg#<id> reference typed into --title is functionally dead: it looks like a deliberate cross-reference but goes nowhere, and the reader has no way to follow it. Refuse it at parse time in the CLI argument parser, in the same branch that already validates --title's value, with a clear error naming the fix (move the reference into the body).

## Why (motivation)
Raised by Alex alongside the matching task-cli and gh-ship request (tg#6109): 'Причём в title вообще запрети инструментально делать такие упоминания, они должны переноситься в тело' -- applies to all three tools he named, tg-cli included, not just the two new ones.

> **tg#6109** — Alex, 2026-07-04 01:37 UTC:
> Упоминания вида tg#5900 в пр не имеет смысла 
> Сделай чтобы task-cli и gh ship умели так же как и tg-cli делать такие упоминания ссылками и цитировать еще 
> Примем в title вообще запрети инструментально делать такие упоминания, они должны переноситься в тело

## User impact
Whoever sends a tg message with --title can no longer accidentally bury a tg#<id> reference somewhere it will never become clickable or quotable -- the tool tells them immediately to put it in the body instead, where the existing autolink feature actually handles it.

## Cost of inaction
A title-embedded tg#<id> silently looks like a working cross-reference in the sent message header but is dead text -- nobody notices until they try to follow it and it goes nowhere.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] the CLI argument parser refuses --title <value> when <value> contains a tg#<id> reference, with a message naming the fix
- [ ] the same reference in the message body (not --title) is unaffected -- only the title is banned

title: pre-send-photo hook: forward outgoing caption as --intent to review visual
body:
## Problem

Alex reported (tg#6188): a HyperCanvas screenshot captioned as showing a "selected"
element passed `review visual` even though no selection outline was drawn.

## Root cause (half of it — the other half is in review-cli#109)

`features/hooks/review-descriptor/pre_send_photo.py` receives the outgoing photo's
caption in the event args (`args.caption`, per the documented `agents-hooks/v1`
contract and `run-photo-hooks.ts`'s `buildEvent`), but never used it: the `review
visual` invocation was always `[review, "visual", image_path, "--json", "--strict"]`
with no `--intent`.

review-cli's intent-gated contributed modules (e.g. `selection-highlight`, the
deterministic CV veto for a missing selection outline) only activate when `--intent`
or `--check` mentions their tag. Since the caption was never forwarded as `--intent` at
all, that whole activation path was INERT for every tg-sent photo — English or Russian,
this bug wasn't purely a language gap, the signal never reached review-cli in the first
place.

## Fix

Forward `args.caption` (stripped, when non-empty) as `--intent` to `review visual`.
`--intent` is documented on review's side as untrusted, read-only free text that can
only TIGHTEN which checks run, never loosen a verdict — forwarding arbitrary caption
text is safe under that existing contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A tg photo send with a caption forwards `--intent <caption>` to `review visual`.
- [ ] A send with no caption (or a blank one) keeps today's argv unchanged (no `--intent`).
- [ ] Non-English (Russian) captions are forwarded byte-for-byte.

## Proof

`tests/hooks-review-descriptor.test.ts`: updated argv assertion + two new tests
(caption forwarded verbatim incl. non-English; blank caption adds no flag).

See also review-cli#109 (alex-mextner/review-cli), the other half of tg#6188: even
once forwarded, the intent-matching itself needed Russian synonyms added.

title: pre-send-photo: _safe_intent() silently drops an unencodable caption without warn()
body:
## Found during

Review of PR #133's merge with #141 (HYP-891), scoped `review diff --pool 1` on
`features/hooks/review-descriptor/pre_send_photo.py`. **Not a regression** —
this behavior is already live on `main` via #141, unchanged; filing as a
follow-up rather than fixing inline in the #133 merge (smallest-change: don't
silently rewrite already-shipped, already-reviewed code as a side effect of an
unrelated merge).

## What's wrong

In `_safe_intent()`:

```python
try:
    text.encode(sys.getfilesystemencoding(), "strict")
except (UnicodeEncodeError, LookupError):
    return ""
```

When a non-empty, non-whitespace caption fails strict encoding (e.g. it
contains a lone UTF-16 surrogate), `_safe_intent` silently returns `""` — no
`warn()` call. `review visual` still runs (correct — verification is not
disabled), but the `--intent` flag is silently dropped with zero trace in
stderr/the audit log.

## Why it matters

The caption is sender-controlled. A crafted caption containing a lone
surrogate silently disables any intent-gated check (e.g. `selection-highlight`'s
hard CV veto, tg#6188) for that specific send, with **no signal anywhere**
that this happened. The PR that introduced `--intent` forwarding (#141)
built its whole safety case on "a spurious block is loud and recoverable... a
silently-passed false positive is not" — this is exactly that silent-failure
shape, just for the intent channel rather than the whole verification call.

## Suggested fix

Add a `warn(...)` call in `_safe_intent` (or at its call site in `main()`)
specifically for the "non-empty caption failed strict encoding" case —
distinct from the already-silent "caption was empty/whitespace-only" case,
which needs no warning. This makes the drop visible in the audit trail
without changing the fail-open behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-empty caption that fails `_safe_intent`'s strict-encode check
      produces a `warn()` line naming that `--intent` was dropped (with a
      reason), while `review visual` still runs.
- [ ] A regression test in `tests/hooks-review-descriptor.test.ts` captures
      stderr for the lone-surrogate case and asserts the warning is present
      (the existing surrogate test only asserts `review visual` still ran,
      not that the drop was logged).

title: Flaky CI: tests/ctl-topic-spawn-integration.test.ts VANISHED-dir re-spawn cases fail intermittently in full suite
body:
## What's wrong

`tests/ctl-topic-spawn-integration.test.ts`'s "re-spawn into a VANISHED dir
restarts the /new flow" family of tests fails intermittently when run as part
of the FULL suite in CI, but passes reliably (3/3) when run in isolation
locally.

## Evidence

Two independent CI failures, on unrelated branches/commits, same test family:

1. `main` branch itself, run 28690695533 (2026-07-04T01:25:29Z, unrelated to
   any pre-send-photo work): `(fail) increment 4: a message to a closed topic
   whose retained dir VANISHED restarts the /new flow, no dead button (codex r6)`
2. PR #133 (`fix/pre-send-photo-remove-window-block`), run 28697995580
   (2026-07-04T06:39:41Z): `(fail) increment 4: re-spawn into a VANISHED dir
   restarts the /new flow (not stuck at awaiting-model) (codex #1)`

Both are different parametrized cases from the same test file/scenario
family. Locally: `bun test tests/ctl-topic-spawn-integration.test.ts -t
"VANISHED"` passes 3/3, run 3 times in a row, in isolation.

This points to a resource-contention / timing issue that only manifests when
run alongside the other ~1900 tests in the same CI process (not a
deterministic logic bug reachable in isolation) — likely a race around the
"vanished directory" simulation (fs mtime/stat timing, or a shared temp path)
that gets slower/less deterministic under full-suite load.

## Impact

Every PR is one unlucky CI run away from a red `test` check on completely
unrelated changes, forcing a re-run rather than a genuine signal. This has
now hit both `main` itself and at least one PR branch.

## Suggested next step

- Identify the exact race (likely in how the "vanished dir" is simulated/
  detected — check for a stat-then-act gap, a shared tmpdir across parallel
  tests, or a timeout that's tight under load).
- Consider isolating this test's fixture directory more strictly, or adding
  a small retry/settle in the test's own setup rather than the assertion.

title: tg-ctl: synchronous unforgeable 'ask & wait for a real Telegram reply' primitive for external approval callers (tg#6554)
body:
## Summary

`tg-ctl` should grow a synchronous, unforgeable **"ask a question and block for a real Telegram reply"** primitive — e.g. `tg-ctl ask "<question>" --timeout <seconds>` — that a *separate* caller process (a pre-bash hook, a CI step, any script) can invoke to get a genuine human yes/no verdict routed through the trusted daemon that already owns the bot's `getUpdates` long-poll.

Motivating context: Alex tg#6554 and agent-tools PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/189.

## Why (the motivating change)

`agent-tools` just replaced the self-service escape hatches in two safety hooks (`pin-primary-worktree`, `block-reset-hard`) with a deny-by-default **external-approval extension point**: `agent_hooks.approval_cmd` in a committed `rig.yaml`. When a block is about to fire, the hook runs that command and allows only on exit 0; nothing configured = denied.

That extension point is deliberately generic (any shell command). The *intended* eventual wiring is: `approval_cmd = "tg-ctl ask 'Agent wants to <X> in <repo> — approve?' --timeout 120"` — so a real destructive/collision-risk operation pauses and asks Alex on his phone, and proceeds only on a genuine tap. **That primitive does not exist yet**, which is why the agent-tools PR ships the extension point but documents the Telegram-backed approver as a future integration rather than faking it.

## Why a naive approach is NOT sufficient (the security requirement)

The whole point is that the caller is a hook meant to **constrain the very agent** running on the same machine. So the "reply" must be verified against the daemon's own live `getUpdates` stream — the single trusted consumer — and must NOT be readable/writable from anything the constrained agent can reach:

- **A hook that polls the local `features/replies` history JSONL is forgeable**: the same agent has shell access and could append a fake `"Alex said yes"` record, or race the file. Unacceptable.
- **A hook calling the Telegram Bot API directly** would fight `tg-ctl` for the single `getUpdates` long-poll consumer slot (only one consumer can drain updates), and still has no trusted binding between "the question I sent" and "the reply I read".

Only `tg-ctl` — the sole process that owns the live `getUpdates` session — can send a question and then authoritatively match an incoming real reply to it. So the primitive has to live **inside `tg-ctl`**, not in the caller.

## Proposed shape (sketch, open to design)

`tg-ctl ask "<question>" [--timeout <s>] [--allow-from <user-id>] [--context <k=v>...]`:

1. Sends `<question>` via the bot (optionally with inline yes/no buttons).
2. **Blocks the calling process** until either:
   - a matching real reply/tap arrives, verified against the daemon's own live `getUpdates` stream and bound to *this* question (correlation id / callback data the daemon issued, not something the caller supplied), from an allowed sender; or
   - `--timeout` elapses.
3. Returns the verdict to the caller via **exit code** (0 = approved, nonzero = denied/timeout) and/or a machine-readable line on stdout (the approver's identity, the matched reply text, a timestamp).

Notes / constraints to work through in design:
- The daemon already injects inbound replies into the agent's tmux pane on the *next* turn; this new path is different — it's a **synchronous** ask/wait for a *third-party* caller, and its reply consumption must not collide with (or leak into) the normal tmux-injection path.
- Correlation must be daemon-issued and unguessable so the constrained agent can't fabricate a matching reply.
- Reasonable default-deny on timeout / no daemon running / not-allowed sender.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `tg-ctl ask` (or agreed equivalent) exists: sends a question, blocks the caller, returns a verdict via exit code, respects `--timeout` with default-deny on timeout.
- [ ] The reply is verified against the daemon's live `getUpdates` stream and bound to the specific question (not read from a caller-writable local file), from an allowed sender.
- [ ] An end-to-end test against a fake Bot API proves: (a) a matching real reply → exit 0; (b) timeout → nonzero; (c) an unrelated/forged local history entry does NOT approve.
- [ ] Docs: how to wire it as an `agent_hooks.approval_cmd` in a consuming repo's `rig.yaml` (closing the loop with the agent-tools extension point).

## User impact of not doing this

Without it, the agent-tools approval extension point can only be wired to a repo-owner shell script (or left unconfigured = hard deny). There is no way to get a live, unforgeable "ask Alex on his phone and wait" gate for genuinely-needed one-off destructive operations — the exact human-in-the-loop primitive the escape-hatch removal was meant to eventually enable.

title: Persistent codex/agent tmux panes have no task-lock — new inbound message silently drops in-flight work
body:
## What
Persistent tmux panes running a long-lived agent process (codex, claude) have no 'task-lock' concept in tg-ctl's inject path. When a NEW inbound message (via tg /agent routing, or a plain reply that resolves to that pane) is injected into a pane that is already mid-task, the underlying agent process treats it as just the next line of the SAME conversation — 'what do I do next' — not as a competing, distinct task. The agent silently abandons whatever it was doing (no commit, no explicit hand-off, no error) and starts on the new request. tg-ctl has no signal today that would tell it the pane is 'busy on task A, this new message is unrelated' vs 'this is a natural continuation of task A'.

## Why (motivation)
2026-07-04: [HYP-915](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-915/preview-should-auto-sample-required-props-before-showing-no-sample) (auto-sample-props heuristic, tg#6408) was dispatched into a persistent codex pane (tmux window '4:3 tg-cli', pane %53) and then sat with ZERO commits for 6 hours. A same-day investigation (traced live by re-running the pane's history) confirmed the root cause: a second, unrelated message — '/agent tg-cli' (tg#6415) — was routed into the SAME pane while codex was still mid-task. codex had no way to distinguish 'new instruction for the current task' from 'a completely different task that happens to share this terminal', so it just switched. Work was eventually recovered via [PR #631](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/631) only because someone noticed the 6-hour silence and manually resumed it — that recovery was luck, not a designed safety net.

> **tg#6408** — Alex, 2026-07-04 12:51 UTC: Такого быть не должно. Должны генериться пропы для семпла детерминированной эвристикой Если есть ии то результаты генера…
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:6408 -->
> **tg#6415** — Alex, 2026-07-04 12:54 UTC: /agent tg-cli Разберись почему у меня уже 98% недельного лимита в клоде а репорт об этом не пришел
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:6415 -->

## User impact
Any dispatch that lands in an already-busy persistent pane can silently stall or derail for an unbounded amount of time, with no error, no status change, and no commit trail — the only way it's caught today is a human noticing 'this has been quiet for suspiciously long' and manually re-prompting. This corrupts task-status tracking (a ticket looks 'in progress' while nothing is happening) and wastes hours per occurrence.

## Cost of inaction
The pattern repeats every time two unrelated topics get addressed into the same persistent codex/agent pane: work stalls or gets silently dropped for an unpredictable window, task status becomes unreliable, and recovery depends on a human noticing the silence rather than any system guarantee.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Before tg-ctl injects a new inbound message into a pane, it checks whether that pane is 'busy' (uncommitted git changes in its cwd, and/or the agent is mid-response rather than idle at a prompt) and, if so, surfaces an explicit git-state-check warning banner back to the sender BEFORE the text is delivered into the pane, instead of silently pasting it in.
- [ ] tg-ctl offers (or the routing picker defaults to) an alternative for messages that don't match the busy pane's current task context: spin up a NEW tmux pane/session for the new topic rather than injecting into the occupied one, so two unrelated tasks never share one prompt.
- [ ] The fix is verified against this exact repro shape: dispatch task A into a pane, then send an unrelated task B into the same pane before A commits — the system must either block/warn instead of silent-switching, or route B to a fresh pane.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- Session: session:0

title: Empty-watermark heuristic never detects a real empty VS Code screenshot
body:
## What's wrong

`looks_like_empty_vscode_watermark()` / `warn_empty_watermark_if_detected()` in
`features/hooks/review-descriptor/pre_send_photo.py` is a WARN-only heuristic
meant to catch a screenshot that shows VS Code's "no tabs open" empty-editor
watermark instead of real content. Investigating why an empty screenshot
passed a visual proof gate undetected (tg#6651, tg#6672) found it returns
`False` on BOTH available real reference screenshots of a genuinely empty VS
Code window.

Every existing test fixture for this detector is synthetic (a ~120-level
contrast fake glyph block on a fake background); the code's own comments
repeatedly note "NOT verified against a captured reference screenshot... none
was available." That gap is now closed with two real screenshots.

## Root cause (measured by direct pixel analysis)

1. The sample box (`WATERMARK_BOX = (0.20, 0.90, 0.15, 0.65)`) physically
   overlaps a docked right panel (e.g. a Chat panel) on a common full-window
   layout. That panel's divider border lines and foreground content -- not the
   actual watermark -- were the "non-bg" signal the detector picked up,
   blowing the measured compactness span to ~0.8-0.93 (rejected, but for the
   wrong reason).
2. Even past that, the real VS Code watermark (current Dark Modern theme) is
   a single flat logo mark whose contrast against the editor background is
   only ~6-7 RGB levels -- completely invisible under the existing
   `WATERMARK_BG_TOL=20`.

## Evidence

Two real screenshots of an empty VS Code window (Explorer + Chat panel
docked, zero editor tabs open) both measure identically:
`non_bg_ratio ≈ 0.116`, `span_x ≈ 0.315`, `span_y ≈ 0.448` once the box is
scoped clear of the side panels and the tolerance is lowered enough to see
the logo -- all outside the current constants' accepted ranges.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `looks_like_empty_vscode_watermark()` returns `True` on both real
      reference screenshots.
- [ ] Full existing test suite (`bun test`) stays green -- no regression on
      the synthetic negative fixtures.
- [ ] Verified against several real BUSY (non-empty) full-window screenshots
      that the recalibrated thresholds do not false-positive.
- [ ] Stays WARN-only, not a block (HYP-891 precedent: an unvalidated pixel
      heuristic hard-blocking a legitimate send is the failure mode this file
      exists to avoid).

## User impact

Without this, the one heuristic specifically designed to flag "this
screenshot may not show what the caption claims" for an empty VS Code editor
never actually fires on the real thing -- silently reducing an intended
audit-trail signal to a no-op for the exact case it was built for.

title: git-state-check banner: warn before a message lands in an occupied pane
body:
## What
tg-ctl checks the destination tmux pane's git state (uncommitted changes / non-main branch) right before a SILENT auto-bind delivery (plain inbound text, a photo/document notice, a standalone voice transcript) and prepends a warning banner when the pane is mid-flight, naming the branch and file count. Config toggle control.git_state_banner (default true).

## Why (motivation)
Root-cause fix for a real incident: an agent working on ticket HYP-915 (a separate, hyperide-repo ticket) appeared to silently drop that task for 6 hours. Cause: tg-ctl routes an inbound Telegram message to a tmux PANE, not to 'the agent current task' -- a fresh, unrelated message landed in the pane mid-flight on HYP-915 and the pane just read it as a continuation of the same conversation, with no signal it was a new, different thread.

## User impact
Whoever or whatever receives a message in an occupied tmux pane (a human reading it, or an AI agent such as Claude Code or Codex) now gets an explicit, harness-agnostic warning when that pane already has feature work in flight, instead of silently treating an unrelated message as more of the same task.

## Cost of inaction
The exact HYP-915 failure mode recurs silently: a new task quietly derails whatever the pane was already doing, with no signal to either the human or the agent that anything went wrong until hours later.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] buildGitStateBanner returns a banner for uncommitted changes or a non-main/master branch, and null for a clean main/master checkout or an undeterminable git state (pure unit tests)
- [ ] A real tg-ctl daemon subprocess, against a real git fixture and a shimmed tmux/ps live pane, actually prepends the banner to the injected text for a dirty feature-branch pane and does NOT for a clean-main or non-repo pane (end-to-end integration test)
- [ ] control.git_state_banner: false fully disables the check (no git spawn, no banner) via the same control: YAML block pattern as the existing topics/private topics flags

title: CI flakiness: 2 integration tests intermittently fail on ubuntu runner
body:
## What
On PR #153's first CI run, 'tests/ctl-new-spawn-integration.test.ts: /new <harness> <name> <task> asks that harness models after path, then spawns that harness' and a 'LATE-DELIVER failure: an unreachable pane keeps the entry retained for a re-tap' test both failed on ubuntu-latest. Neither test touches code from that PR's diff. A re-run of the same job passed cleanly with no code changes, so this reads as CI-runner-timing flakiness (real subprocess/tmux-style integration tests under resource contention), not a real regression.

## Why (motivation)
Flaky integration tests erode trust in the green-CI merge gate: a real regression could hide behind an assumed known-flaky retry, and a genuinely clean PR forces an unnecessary manual re-run to get a mergeable state.

## User impact
Whoever opens a PR against this repo (Alex or an agent) sometimes sees a red CI check on a genuinely correct change and has to manually click re-run and wait again before they can merge, instead of trusting a green check the first time.

## Cost of inaction
People keep burning time on unnecessary manual CI re-runs, and eventually a real regression could slip through mislabeled as 'known flaky' and get merged unreviewed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The two named tests pass reliably across at least 10 consecutive CI runs (or a root cause - e.g. a fixed timing budget too tight for the ubuntu runner - is identified and fixed)
- [ ] If a root cause is found, the fix is documented in the test file (why the old timing was insufficient)

title: Escalation-format gate: pre-send-text hook + question tag (tg-cli core)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
CTO-approved design (brainstormed) so that decision/question escalations sent to the CTO over Telegram arrive as structured, scannable asks instead of free-text walls the CTO has to re-derive.

## User impact
When someone (a person or an AI agent) needs a real decision from the CTO, the message they send will nudge them to lay out the choice as a fill-in table (options, tradeoffs, recommendation) instead of a paragraph the CTO has to re-read three times to find the actual question.

## Cost of inaction
Escalations keep landing as unstructured prose; the CTO has to re-derive the actual question and options from a wall of text every time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The 'question' tag is accepted by --tag and renders with the same badge style as 'decision'.
- [ ] A new pre-send-text hook point fires on every tg text send, mirroring the existing pre-send-photo hook plumbing (same timeout, on_error and audit-log framework).
- [ ] An escalation-format hook runs in warn (non-blocking) mode: for --tag decision or question, it detects whether the message body contains a literal table and prints an actionable, self-contained warning (with copy-pasteable table rows and a bypass note) without stopping the send.
- [ ] A cheap parse-time check in the CLI argument parser catches the obvious no-table-anywhere case before any subprocess runs, using a small per-tag gate registry instead of another hardcoded if-branch.
- [ ] The audit log records which tag triggered the gate, what was missing, and a body hash, and the audit log file is rotated instead of growing forever.

title: Escalation gate follow-ups: e2e block test, Tier-2 reachability note, minor edge cases
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Follow-up from the tg-164 escalation-format-gate PR's multi-round AI code review (Opus/Codex/Gemini/GLM). These are real but low-severity findings (documentation gaps + one missing integration test) that were deliberately deferred to keep the main PR mergeable rather than open-ended.

## User impact
A future maintainer reading the escalation-format-gate code without this context could waste time re-discovering that the warn-mode hook is currently dormant in normal use, or ship a regression in the tg-entrypoint block/exit-10 wiring undetected because no test exercises it end to end.

## Cost of inaction
The same review findings resurface independently later, and a real regression in the pre-send-text blocking path (once installed/enabled) could ship silently since nothing tests it end to end.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A subprocess-level test drives the real tg binary with an installed pre-send-text descriptor that exits 10, and asserts tg exits 10 and never calls transmit (closing the gap: today only gateText/runPreSendTextHooks are unit-tested, not the actual loop-and-exit wiring in the tg entrypoint).
- [ ] A code comment on the reference escalation-format-gate hook script documents that its warn branch is currently unreachable through the normal tg CLI flow (Tier 1 in args.ts already hard-blocks the same no-table case at parse time first) — it only fires for a programmatic hook-framework caller or when Tier 1's pre-render caption and Tier 2's final post-render body disagree.
- [ ] The escalation-format gate documents (or fixes) two accepted minor edge cases: (a) a fallback-path audit append bypasses rotation/trim under sustained lock contention, so audit.jsonl can briefly exceed MAX_AUDIT_LINES; (b) when a tg send plan carries multiple separate text messages (e.g. a line-spec quote alongside the main body), each is gated with the SAME --tag, so a tableless auxiliary message can trigger a false warn from the escalation hook.

title: tg-ctl /new private-topic spawn leaks an orphan forum topic and binding on each retry
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
spawnNewSession always calls createPrivateTopic(session.name) when privateTopics is on, even on retry, so each retry creates a new topic plus preliminary binding and orphans the previous threadId binding (spawnPending=false, so reconcile-on-startup refuses to adopt it). Pre-existing on the model re-tap path; the new Retry button makes rapid retries cheap and amplifies the leak.

## User impact
Users on private_topics who hit a spawn failure and retry accumulate dead forum topics and stale awaiting-model bindings that are never cleaned up.

## Cost of inaction
The topic store and the chat slowly fill with orphaned topics and bindings, cluttering the forum and making the /new flow harder to debug.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A failed private-topic /new spawn that is retried reuses the already-created forum topic and preliminary binding instead of minting a new one
- [ ] A private-topics integration test fails a spawn, taps Retry, and asserts exactly one topic and one binding exist afterward (no orphans)

title: tg-ctl /new is broken: tmux index collision, ignored inline dir, fixed arg order, and a re-ask loop on spawn failure
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The daemon spawn built 'tmux new-window -t bare-session'; a numerically-named session made tmux read the target as a window index and abort. The parser only accepted a directory before the name and one post-name selector. On spawn failure the flow re-asked the model, looping the user while the real error scrolled away. Reported repeatedly by the CTO from the live bot.

## User impact
Every /new in a numerically-named tmux session fails; users must re-type the working directory even when they supplied it; out-of-order arguments are silently dropped; a transient spawn failure traps the user in a question loop with no visible error.

## Cost of inaction
The /new command remains unusable in the CTO daily setup and keeps generating repeat bug reports.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tmux new-window targets the session unambiguously so a numeric session name (e.g. a session named 1) no longer fails with 'create window failed: index 1 in use'
- [ ] an inline absolute directory after the name is used and skips the pick-a-project prompt; the parser accepts its arguments in any order; only missing pieces are asked
- [ ] a spawn failure reports the real error once and offers a Retry button that preserves the chosen answers, and never re-asks in a loop

title: tg-ctl: graceful reload — no dropped channel across restart
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Restarting the daemon dropped the live Telegram channel: the in-memory defer-while-waiting backlog was lost, and immediate SIGTERM cleanExit dropped the in-flight getUpdates batch (at-most-once). Alex talks to agents through this daemon, so a restart cut live conversations.

## User impact
Before this fix, a person mid-conversation on Telegram loses the messages they already sent, and the daemon skips updates, every time the daemon restarts or reloads.

## Cost of inaction
Every tg-ctl reload keeps silently dropping queued messages and in-flight updates; the rig auto-reload-on-commit feature would make this happen on every commit.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No queued/deferred message is lost across a reload: the defer-while-waiting backlog is persisted to disk and restored on bootstrap; restored questions flush their restored backlog on answer.
- [ ] No pending question is dropped across a reload (already durable via the questions store; unchanged).
- [ ] No Telegram update is missed across the swap: SIGTERM cooperatively drains the in-flight getUpdates batch before exit instead of an immediate cleanExit; offset stays durable.
- [ ] Full bun test suite is green, including new deferred-store round-trip/fail-closed/pane-cap tests and DeferQueues snapshot/restore tests.

title: tg-ctl: graceful reload preserves queued inbound messages
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The daemon kept the wait-queue only in memory, so any daemon exit silently dropped messages a person had already sent, forcing them to resend.

## User impact
When you send a message to an agent while it is waiting on its own question, that message no longer disappears if the tg-ctl bridge restarts or reloads underneath you. You do not have to notice the drop or resend it; the bridge picks up exactly where it left off.

## Cost of inaction
Every bridge restart or reload keeps silently swallowing messages people already sent, so they lose trust in the Telegram bridge and have to re-type lost messages.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Messages a person sends that are queued behind an agent's open question are saved to disk when queued and re-loaded when the daemon starts again, so restarting or reloading the tg-ctl bridge loses none of them.
- [ ] The saved queue is versioned and fail-safe: a corrupted or unknown-version file is ignored (the daemon starts with an empty queue) and never crashes startup; empty queues are not resurrected; a per-pane cap bounds the file size.
- [ ] The full bun test suite is green (2252 pass, 0 fail), including new tests for the durable store and the save/restore round-trip.

title: /tasks: a failing 'task list' renders as an empty board (log-only, not surfaced to the user)
body:
Carried forward from PR #135 (chatgpt-codex-connector P2, originally on #129).

**Finding.** In \`tg-ctl\`, \`loadTaskList\` (and \`loadPrRefs\`) return \`[]\` on a non-zero exit / malformed JSON and only \`log(...)\` the failure to the daemon log. The user then sees a normal "No matching tasks" board — a genuine failure (missing \`task\` binary, invalid scoped cwd, unsupported flags) is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty backlog.

**Status vs #135's two findings.**
- Finding 1 (unmatched \`/tasks <agent>\` selector silently scoped to daemon cwd) — **already fixed in main**: \`resolveTasksScopeDir\` returns \`null\` on a non-confident match and \`runTasksCommand\` replies \`couldn't resolve a project for /tasks <agent> …\`.
- Finding 2 (this issue) — **NOT surfaced to the user in main.** Main logs but still renders an empty board.

**Why this is a separate follow-up, not folded during the #135 cleanup.** Surfacing the failure means threading an error (#135 used \`{ tasks, error }\`) through the \`loadTasks\` state fan-out → \`runTasksCommand\` → the view composer, i.e. a semantic behavior change to the shared, working #179/#120 tasks-board code. Both \`loadTaskList\` and \`loadPrRefs\` use the same deliberate log-and-return-\`[]\` pattern, so this is a product decision on shared code, not a mechanical port. Deferred rather than guessed at.

**Acceptance.** A failing/malformed \`task list\` (or \`gh pr list\`) surfaces a distinct operator-visible signal on the board instead of an empty "No matching tasks" view; a blank-but-successful stdout stays a legitimate empty backlog. TDD, red-first (\`tests/ctl-tasks-error-integration.test.ts\` in #135 is a ready reference).

title: tg silently fragments an oversized message into dozens of separate Telegram sends instead of warning or refusing
body:
Reproduced 2026-07-18. An orchestrator's Bash-invoked `tg --format html ...` call had an accidental shell command-substitution bug in its message body (unrelated root cause, already tracked separately) that caused the body to balloon from ~1.4KB to ~34KB. `tg` sent this without any size check — Telegram's own ~4096-char message limit caused the send to fragment into 82 separate messages, delivered in about 17 seconds, which read to the recipient as an incoherent flood/spam and made the actual content nearly impossible to follow.

Ask: add a sanity cap independent of *why* a body got large — e.g., refuse to send (or require an explicit --allow-long/similar flag) when a message would fragment into more than some small threshold (e.g. 5-6) separate Telegram messages, and instead print a clear local error telling the caller the body is N characters / would produce M messages, so they can fix the input rather than have it silently flood the recipient. A truncate-with-"...output truncated, see logs"-style fallback would also be reasonable, whichever fits tg's existing design better.

title: tg-cli: decode text escapes before enforcing escalation format on --tag decision/question
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The escalation-format gate in tg-cli#202 validates the raw argv caption before the entrypoint's decodeTextEscapes() runs, so tg's supported \n escape sequences are seen as literal backslash-n rather than a newline.

## User impact
A caller using the documented \n-escape convention for a compliant decision-request message gets falsely blocked by the new deny-by-default gate, even though the message is correctly formatted once decoded.

## Cost of inaction
The escalation format gate this PR ships has a false-positive-block edge case for a documented, supported input convention.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The escalation-format gate validates the body AFTER decodeTextEscapes() runs, not the raw argv, so a compliant multiline escalation passed as one shell argument with literal \n escapes is recognized instead of being seen as one pipe-containing line and falsely blocked.
- [ ] A regression test sends a valid decision-request body via a single-argument \n-escaped caption and asserts it passes the gate instead of being rejected as missing sections.

title: tg-cli: skip fenced code blocks when auto-converting markdown pipe tables
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The markdown-pipe-table auto-convert added in tg-cli#202 collects pipe rows from the whole message body without excluding fenced or code regions, so an ordinary markdown example block containing a pipe table gets corrupted into rich-message HTML.

## User impact
A report or docs message that intentionally shows a markdown table as an example inside a code fence gets silently rewritten and forced into a rich send, corrupting the exact content the sender meant to display verbatim.

## Cost of inaction
Any report containing a markdown table code example breaks on send, with no workaround short of avoiding the feature entirely.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The pipe-table-to-HTML converter tracks fenced, preformatted, and inline-code regions and does not treat pipe lines inside a code fence as a real table to convert.
- [ ] A regression test sends a message containing a fenced markdown code block with a pipe-table-shaped example inside it and asserts the fence content is sent verbatim, not rewritten to a table.

title: tg-ctl: migrate pre-existing fully-installed hook setups to the opt-in sentinel
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The self-heal startup path added in tg-cli#204 returns not-opted-in before reading settings.json whenever the sentinel file is absent, so it never migrates a pre-existing fully-installed hook setup created before this sentinel existed.

## User impact
An upgraded user who installed hooks before this feature shipped keeps the advertised self-heal disabled until they manually rerun install-hooks, with no signal that anything is missing.

## Cost of inaction
The self-heal feature silently does not apply to any pre-existing install, undermining the reliability guarantee it advertises for exactly the users most likely to have stale hooks.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A user whose ~/.claude/settings.json already contains all tg-ctl hooks (installed before the claude-hooks-installed sentinel existed) is recognized as opted-in on daemon startup, instead of being classified not-opted-in and left out of self-heal.
- [ ] A regression test simulates a fully-installed settings.json with no sentinel present and asserts the daemon either treats it as opted-in or writes the sentinel once, rather than silently leaving self-heal disabled.

title: tg-ctl: preserve a symlinked ~/.claude/settings.json during hook self-heal write
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The self-heal write added in tg-cli#204 uses tg-ctl's writeAtomic (settings.json.tmp then renameSync over settingsPath), which unlinks a symlink and writes a new regular file in its place; manual install-hooks instead uses writeFileSync, which writes through the symlink and preserves it.

## User impact
A user with a dotfile-managed ~/.claude/settings.json (a common symlink-based dotfiles setup) has their symlink silently replaced by a plain file the first time unattended self-heal fires, breaking their dotfile management.

## Cost of inaction
Dotfile-managed Claude settings setups regress the moment self-heal runs, with no error surfaced -- just a symlink quietly becoming a regular file.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The self-heal write path resolves the real path of a symlinked ~/.claude/settings.json (or otherwise special-cases a symlink) before its atomic rename, instead of unlinking the symlink and replacing it with a new regular file.
- [ ] A regression test creates settings.json as a symlink to a target file, runs the self-heal write, and asserts the symlink itself still points at the same target afterward, matching the manual install-hooks write-through behavior.

title: tg: don't hard-block Cyrillic-affixed acronyms like antiDDoS-style mixed-script tech terms
body:
## What

The mixed-script guard added in tg-cli#206 classifies any run with 2+ script transitions as mojibake, but a legitimate Russian tech term with a Cyrillic prefix and suffix around a Latin acronym also has 2+ transitions and gets the same hard block.

A user writing ordinary Russian tech vocabulary that wraps an English acronym gets their message blocked outright, with no option short of disabling the whole mixed-script guard feature.

The guard keeps producing false-positive hard blocks on a common, legitimate mixed-script writing pattern in Russian tech communication.

title: tg: make escalation-format section validation actually section-aware
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The validator added in tg-cli#202 checks for the presence of a table or a list, heading, or divider anywhere in the body rather than validating that each required section actually has the required content, so cosmetically-shaped-but-empty escalations pass the deny-by-default gate.

## User impact
A sender can satisfy the escalation-format gate with a technically-shaped but practically useless decision request such as an empty single-option table or two headings with no real recommendation, defeating the gate's purpose of ensuring the human can decide in 30 seconds.

## Cost of inaction
The deny-by-default escalation gate gives a false sense of quality enforcement while letting through malformed decision requests that merely mimic the required shape.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The decision-request format validator parses required sections (Options, Recommendation, Where to look) by their own boundaries instead of accepting any table or any two list items anywhere in the body.
- [ ] A regression test proves each of these is rejected: unrelated bullets satisfying the Options requirement, a single-option table, a body with only two headings and one divider and no real content, and a table with no pros or cons filled in.

title: tg: require a real file:line, not just a path, in the escalation-format where-to-look field
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The where-to-look check added in tg-cli#202 makes the line-number suffix optional and accepts any slashed path, while the documented contract everywhere else requires file:line.

## User impact
A person receiving a decision-request message gets sent a bare filename instead of the promised precise line to look at, so they still have to search the file themselves before they can decide.

## Cost of inaction
The gate's documented file:line guarantee is not actually enforced, undermining the reason the where-to-look field exists.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The where-to-look validation in the decision-request format validator requires a numeric line-number suffix, matching the file:line contract advertised in the changelog, help text, and install-skill docs.
- [ ] A regression test proves an extension-only or path-only reference (no line number) is rejected, while a genuine file:line reference still passes.

title: tg: convert every markdown pipe table in a message, not just the first
body:
## What

The converter added in tg-cli#202 returns early whenever detectTableKind sees an existing HTML or boxed table anywhere in the message, so a markdown grid appearing later in the same body is left as literal pipe text instead of being auto-converted.

## User impact

## Cost of inaction
The auto-convert feature silently fails on any message that also happens to contain another table earlier in the body.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The pipe-table-to-HTML converter scans each contiguous block of the message independently and converts every markdown pipe table found, instead of returning early the moment it sees any existing HTML or boxed table earlier in the body.
- [ ] A regression test sends a message containing both an existing HTML table and a separate markdown pipe table later in the body, and asserts the pipe table is converted while the existing HTML table is left alone.

title: tg: harden pipe-table rendering for ragged rows and tighten the where-to-look file reference check
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A fresh review pass on tg-cli#202 found the pipe-table renderer does not normalize ragged column counts, the file-reference regex accepts common non-path tokens as if they were file:line pointers, and the escalation gate never considers --items even though that flag exists specifically for attaching file references.

## User impact
A person sending a report with an uneven markdown table can get a corrupted or rejected Telegram table, and a person relying on --items to supply their file reference gets falsely blocked by the escalation gate even though they did point at a file.

## Cost of inaction
Table rendering stays fragile for a common authoring mistake, and the where-to-look check stays close to a no-op for ordinary prose while blocking a legitimate --items-based reference.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The pipe-table-to-HTML converter pads or truncates data rows to the header's column count, and skips a degenerate empty row instead of emitting an empty <tr> or a mismatched-cell-count row.
- [ ] The where-to-look file-reference pattern in the escalation-format validator no longer matches ordinary non-path tokens such as and/or, A/B, or a time like 12:30 as a valid file reference.
- [ ] The --items feature (file references passed via --items rather than in the caption) is either fed into the escalation-format validator so it can satisfy the where-to-look requirement, or the gate's help text explicitly states that --items content does not count.

title: tg: document how to compose a compliant decision or question escalation via tg --table
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Verified empirically that a compliant --tag decision --table send is possible today (a fully-structured --format html heading text around the boxed table passes validateEscalationFormat), but nothing documents this and the only existing test shows the BLOCKED bare-table case, leaving the compliant path undiscoverable.

## User impact
A person who wants to send a decision request with a real data table has no example showing how to actually satisfy the gate, and might reasonably conclude (incorrectly) that --table cannot be used for escalations at all.

## Cost of inaction
Users hit the block on a bare --table escalation and have no path forward beyond disabling the gate, even though a compliant shape exists.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The --table help text or the escalation-format gate's guidance shows a copy-pasteable example of a compliant --tag decision send using --table, since the argv heading (with --format html) is where the Context, Recommendation, and Where-to-look sections must live around the boxed table.
- [ ] A passing subprocess test demonstrates this exact compliant --table shape sends without a block, alongside the existing test proving a bare --table decision still blocks.

## Screenshots

title: tg: escalation-format validator structure checks have false-positive and false-negative edge cases
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A fresh review pass on tg-cli#202 found the structure validator's line-based heuristics misclassify a valid single-line HTML escalation as a wall of text, misclassify a real bullet list as an inline comma-run false positive, and the entrypoint's --table structure check hardcodes the tag names instead of reusing the shared escalation-tags list.

## User impact
A person composing a valid escalation as one shell-argument line, or using a legitimate labelled bullet list, can get falsely blocked by the deny-by-default gate with no way to fix a report that already follows the required shape; and a future third escalation tag would silently skip the --table structure check.

## Cost of inaction
The deny-by-default gate keeps producing false-positive blocks on valid input shapes, and the tag list drifts out of sync as new escalation tags are added.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A compliant escalation body written as ONE line of HTML (no newlines between sections) passes the wall-of-text check instead of being flagged as a run-on, by measuring block-level content rather than raw line length.
- [ ] A genuine bullet list whose label line contains a colon and three or more comma-separated items on one line (e.g. a Pros heading followed by list items) is not misclassified as an inline comma-run.
- [ ] The hardcoded decision-or-question tag check in the entrypoint's post-render validation uses the same ESCALATION_TAGS list the parse-time gate is built from, instead of a separately hardcoded pair of tag names.

## Screenshots
(none)

title: tg: reconcile mixed-script-guard docs with its actual bidirectional detection
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The mixed-script guard shipped in tg-cli#206 documents catching only a foreign fragment sandwiched inside Cyrillic, e.g. почčesна, but verified empirically that a Cyrillic letter sandwiched inside a foreign-script word (e.g. mir with a Cyrillic i in the middle) is also flagged, since the detector counts script transitions symmetrically.

## User impact
A person reading the tool's own documentation to understand what gets blocked gets an incomplete picture, and might be surprised when a token they expected to pass (because it doesn't match the documented one-directional example) gets blocked anyway.

## Cost of inaction
The documentation keeps describing a narrower guard than what actually ships, undermining trust in the docs for this feature.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The README, changelog, and JSDoc for the mixed-script guard either state clearly that it catches BOTH Cyrillic-sandwiches-foreign and foreign-sandwiches-Cyrillic token shapes, or the detector is narrowed to only the documented Cyrillic-sandwiches-foreign direction.
- [ ] A CLI regression test covers whichever directionality is chosen as the final documented contract (a foreign-Cyrillic-foreign token like mir with a Cyrillic middle letter).

## Screenshots
(none)

title: tg: report the mixed-script guard's offending-token position against the authored input, not the rendered table
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The mixed-script guard added in tg-cli#206 scans the rendered <pre> table (which is prefixed with box-drawing characters and padding) rather than the raw stdin the user typed, so a token in the first cell reports a position far past where it actually appears in what the user typed.

## User impact
A person trying to locate and fix the flagged token in their original table input gets pointed at the wrong character offset, since the reported position is measured in the generated table markup instead of their own typed text.

## Cost of inaction
The position hint in the error message stays actively misleading for any --table send, making the error harder to act on than it should be.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When the mixed-script guard scans a --table send's rendered pre-formatted output, the reported character position points at the offending token's location in the ORIGINAL stdin table input the user typed, not the position within the generated box-drawing markup.
- [ ] A CLI regression test sends a --table body with a mixed-script token in the first data cell and asserts the reported position matches where that token appears in the raw stdin, not an inflated offset from the rendered pre block's box-drawing characters.

## Screenshots
(none)

title: tg: mixed-script guard hard-blocks common Russian dev slang like zapushil, zadeployil (Cyrillic prefix plus English verb stem plus Cyrillic suffix)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Verified empirically that the mixed-script guard shipped in tg-cli#206 flags zapushil, zamergeil, zacommitil, and otdebugil as mixed-script garbage and hard-blocks the send, because each is one contiguous letter run with two script transitions (Cyrillic to Latin to Cyrillic), the exact shape the guard is designed to catch -- but this is also the shape of a common Russian tech-slang word-formation pattern (a Cyrillic grammatical prefix and suffix wrapped around an English verb kept in Latin script), not garbled mojibake.

## User impact
A Russian-speaking developer using their own normal technical vocabulary in a message gets hard-blocked from sending it, with no way to fix the wording (the words are already correctly spelled) short of disabling the entire guard feature and losing the stray-CJK protection along with it.

## Cost of inaction
The guard actively breaks a realistic, everyday Russian dev-slang writing pattern for its primary user base, turning a safety feature into a recurring annoyance that trains people to just disable it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Verified real Russian developer slang words that glue a Cyrillic prefix and suffix onto an untransliterated English verb stem (za-push-il, za-merge-il, za-commit-il, ot-debug-il) no longer hard-block as mixed-script garbage, while the original motivating mojibake case (pochchesna) still blocks.
- [ ] A regression test pins the chosen resolution with the exact verified false-positive words from this finding, alongside the existing mojibake-blocking test case.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: tg: mixed-script guard is bypassable via invisible format characters splitting a run
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Verified the mixed-script guard's run-splitting logic treats any non-letterish codepoint, including invisible Unicode format characters, as a run boundary, so a mojibake token with a stray zero-width space or soft hyphen inserted splits into two single-transition segments and passes the guard silently.

## User impact
A person receiving a garbled AI-generated message doesn't get the protection this guard promises, because a stray invisible character in the garbled text quietly lets it through instead of being caught and rejected before it's sent.

## Cost of inaction
The guard has a known, verified blind spot for exactly the kind of malformed text it exists to block.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The mixed-script guard treats format control characters (zero-width space, zero-width non-joiner, soft hyphen, and similar Unicode Cf characters) the same way it treats combining marks -- riding along inside a letter run without resetting the transition count -- so an LLM-emitted mojibake token with an invisible character inserted no longer slips past the guard.
- [ ] A regression test proves a token with a zero-width space (or another Cf character) inserted into an otherwise-blocked mojibake shape still gets blocked.

title: transmit() preflight refusals (rich-HTML / flood-cap) leak pdfTempDirs via process.exit
body:
## Context

Found during review of #207/#208 (PR fixing missing/empty/unreadable attachments and the message-flood cap), by two independent review-cli passes (Codex, both rounds).

`transmit()`'s preflight checks (`preflightRichHtml`, `preflightFloodCap` in `features/auto-attach/transmitter.ts`) call `process.exit(1)` directly on a refusal. In the `tg` entrypoint, `code-as-pdf`/`md-as-pdf` conversion can populate `pdfTempDirs` (temp directories holding rendered PDFs) BEFORE `transmit()` is called. Cleanup of `pdfTempDirs` happens AFTER `await transmit(...)` returns — but `process.exit()` never returns, so that cleanup is unreachable whenever a preflight refuses the send after a PDF was already rendered.

Net effect: a send that (a) has a code/markdown attachment that gets rendered to a PDF, AND (b) is ALSO refused by the rich-HTML validator or the flood cap, leaves an orphaned temp directory (containing the rendered PDF) under `/tmp` (or `$TMPDIR`) that is never cleaned up.

## Why it wasn't fixed in #207/#208's PR

This is a pre-existing pattern (the rich-HTML preflight had the identical characteristic before that PR touched anything) — the flood-cap preflight just adds a second path with the same shape, not a new category of bug. Fixing it properly means either:
1. Making `transmit()`'s preflights return a typed refusal instead of calling `process.exit()` directly, so the `tg` entrypoint can run `pdfTempDirs` cleanup in a `finally` before exiting — this changes `transmit()`'s contract and would need every existing `process.exit` mock-based test updated.
2. Or moving preflight validation entirely before PDF conversion runs — which requires duplicating (or restructuring) the caption-riding decision that the flood cap depends on, since that's currently computed from the POST-conversion, POST-filter plan.

Both are a larger, riskier change than the targeted #207/#208 fix, so this is being tracked separately rather than bundled in.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A send with a code/markdown attachment that renders to a PDF, followed by a refused preflight (invalid rich HTML, or the flood cap), does not leave an orphaned temp directory under `$TMPDIR`.
- [ ] Existing `transmit()` tests (rich-HTML refusal, flood-cap refusal) still pass unchanged in shape (still exit non-zero, still send nothing).

## User impact

Low severity — a rare combination (PDF-convertible attachment + a send that ALSO gets refused for an unrelated reason) leaves a few stray files under `/tmp`. Not a crash, not data loss, self-limiting (most systems periodically clean `/tmp`), but worth closing properly rather than leaving as tribal knowledge.

body:
## What

Alex (CTO) repeatedly hit two confusing tg-ctl messages: an unidentifiable 'hook disconnected — tap after the agent reconnects' card that gave no clue which agent it was about, overclaimed a guaranteed reconnect, and silently swallowed a permission tap when the hook never came back; and a usage-limit warning that told him to redeem a 'banked/earned reset via /usage' even when he was on Claude, which has no such mechanic.

title: tg-ctl: stale abandoned question/permission entries not reaped from questions.json store
body:
## What
When a forwarded question/permission's hook socket closes, tg-ctl retains a SCOPED
(paneId-set) entry in the in-memory abandonedButtons map (and persists it to
~/.config/tg-cli/tg-ctl.<botId>.questions.json) so a late Telegram tap can still
reach the pane or a reconnecting hook can re-attach. This retention is deliberate
(see tg-ctl's retainAbandonedQuestion / armPendingSocketClose), not itself the bug.

The bug is in reaping: two mechanisms are supposed to drop an abandoned entry once
it is older than ABANDONED_RETAIN_MS (30 minutes by default) — (1) a per-mutation
prune inside persistQuestions(), and (2) a periodic sweep in the daemon's main poll
loop (checks abandonedButtons.size, calls pruneAbandonedButtons, then persists if
anything changed), called roughly every ~50s long-poll cycle. Neither fired for a
real production entry.

Concrete repro (verified on the live machine, not synthetic):
- requestId claude-1d95y0e, pane %2 (tmux session ext-claude, cwd
  /Users/ultra/work/hyperide), a Bash permission ask forwarded and posted as
  Telegram message 9975.
- Daemon log: "ask-forward posted: ... req=claude-1d95y0e ... messageId=9975" at
  2026-07-22T16:43:44.348Z (UTC), then "question released on %2 — no queued
  message(s)" at 2026-07-22T16:45:39.143Z — the hook socket closed without ever
  receiving a Telegram answer (it was resolved some other way, e.g. answered
  directly in the terminal), landing this entry in abandonedButtons with
  at: 1784738739143 (2026-07-22 18:45:39 local).
- ~/.config/tg-cli/tg-ctl.8574086668.questions.json still contains this exact
  entry, byte-identical, and its mtime is frozen at "Jul 22 18:45:39" — i.e. the
  file has NOT been rewritten once since the release, even though it is now
  2026-07-23T10:13 (about 15.5 hours later, roughly 31x past the 30-minute
  retention window).
- This is NOT a case of the daemon being down or idle-exited: the daemon process
  (pid 91212) has been continuously running since well before the event (started
  Thursday 1pm per ps), and its log shows plenty of unrelated activity in between
  (route/inject lines the same evening, an HTTP 502 plus a poll-loop timeout error
  the next night, and more activity this morning) — so the main loop was clearly
  iterating throughout. Despite that, the log has zero "ask-abandoned-long-outage"
  line for this requestId, ever — that is the exact line the daemon logs when the
  periodic sweep or persist-time prune actually drops an entry past its retention
  window.
- Net effect: the persisted store accumulates entries that silently outlive their
  own documented retention window indefinitely once this happens, and the Telegram
  card (message 9975) was left showing the "abandoned" text with its inline
  keyboard still attached — the release-time edit does not clear the keyboard,
  only the long-outage notice path does, and that path never ran — so the card may
  still look tappable long after it stopped being deliverable.

Suggested fix direction (not applied — filing only):
- Instrument/trace why the prune-and-persist sweep did not drop this entry despite
  being reachable and the loop demonstrably iterating for 15+ hours afterward —
  verify the size-changed gate in the poll loop actually runs every iteration and
  is not short-circuited by an earlier exception/return in the same loop body, and
  check whether some other code path re-inserts or refreshes this entry's
  timestamp without logging.
- Once the reap path is confirmed reliable, consider a defense-in-depth periodic
  sweep independent of the size-based gate (e.g. always log a debug line each
  sweep tick) so a future regression here is observable from logs alone.

## Why (motivation)
Investigating an unrelated tg-ctl question found a real production entry (requestId claude-1d95y0e, Telegram message 9975) that sat unpruned in questions.json for 15.5+ hours, roughly 31x past the 30-minute ABANDONED_RETAIN_MS, with the daemon verifiably alive and looping the whole time (log shows unrelated activity before, during, and after the window) — so the documented periodic-sweep plus persist-time-prune reap mechanism is not firing reliably in practice.

## User impact
Stale abandoned question/permission cards can sit in Telegram indefinitely looking tappable (keyboard not cleared) long after they stopped being deliverable, and the on-disk store accumulates stale entries without bound over the life of a long-running daemon, defeating the documented age-based hygiene design.

## Cost of inaction
The persisted questions.json store keeps growing with dead entries indefinitely on any long-running daemon, and a user tapping a long-stale card gets a confusing expired response instead of the daemon having already visibly given up on it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A synthetic or real abandoned scoped question/permission entry is pruned from both the in-memory abandonedButtons map and the on-disk questions.json file within one poll-loop cycle after ABANDONED_RETAIN_MS elapses, even when the daemon receives unrelated activity in the interim, with a passing regression test covering this exact interleaving.
- [ ] The Telegram card for a reaped entry has its inline keyboard cleared at the moment of reap, not only when a stale tap is later attempted.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: false positives: #9975 is a Telegram message id (not an issue ref); size-before/size-after, re-inserts/refreshes, MAX_RETAINED_QUESTIONS/age-based, reply-route/inject/agent-route are code identifiers and log-line names, not repo paths

title: tg-ctl: no relay of agent's post-completion follow-up work back to Telegram (silent open thread despite work being done)
body:
## What
Add a general relay of an agent's turn conclusion back to Telegram, or a documented + surfaced limitation, for interactions that don't hit the existing question/permission/failure hooks. Concrete repro: Telegram message id 9250 (text `!gh ship 61`), sent 2026-07-17 14:37:52 (Europe/Belgrade). Daemon log confirms successful routing/injection: recognized=true sameProject=true, delivered into tmux pane %5 at that timestamp. Pane %5's live session DID eventually work the underlying problem in-session (captured pane content shows discussion like "...so gh ship 61 still refuses... wrong worktree... corrected command given..."), but zero agent/reply messages were ever logged back to Telegram for that pane afterward. As of 2026-07-23 (6 days later) pane %5 is still alive (tmux session 1, window 2, title "os") and the Telegram thread remains open/unanswered. Root cause confirmed by reading the code: hook-install.ts (features/tg-ctl/hook-install.ts) installs exactly four Claude Code hook channels: PreToolUse matcher AskUserQuestion, PermissionRequest matcher star, StopFailure matcher star (harness failure and rate-limit notify), and Stop (codex usage-telemetry only, desiredCodexUsageGroups). There is no hook for a normal successful Stop that relays a turn's conclusion back to Telegram. routes.ts (features/tg-ctl/routes.ts) is purely inbound-reply-to-pane bookkeeping (recognizing which pane a reply routes to based on prior tg sends) and never reads pane output back. updates.ts (features/tg-ctl/updates.ts) textAction, around line 496, injects a leading-bang message VERBATIM into the pane using the harness's OWN bang-at-column-0 shell-passthrough convention; tg-ctl's job ends at injection, it never captures that command's output or the agent's subsequent conversation. So for this whole class (a bang passthrough, or any message whose resulting turn ends normally without those three hook types firing), the only way Telegram hears back is if the agent explicitly remembers to run tg itself before ending its turn; if it doesn't, the thread is silent forever with no error and no timeout signal. Suggested directions: (a) a genuine Stop-success hook channel mirroring StopFailure's pattern that posts a summary or nudge back to the originating route when no explicit tg send happened during the turn; (b) a watchdog over the routes.ts data that flags panes with an inbound message older than N minutes and no corresponding outbound tg send, nudging the user instead of silence; (c) at minimum, document this loudly so it is not mistaken for a delivery bug.

## Why (motivation)
hook-install.ts installs exactly four Claude Code hook channels and none of them cover a normal successful Stop; routes.ts and the bang passthrough in updates.ts confirm tg-ctl never reads pane output back into Telegram outside those hooks, so a resolved problem in a pane produces zero signal back to the user unless the agent remembers to call tg itself.

## User impact
Alex sends a message via Telegram, it is successfully injected and the agent genuinely resolves the problem in-pane, but his phone shows the thread as open and unanswered indefinitely with no way to distinguish silently-failed from quietly-done short of manually opening the pane.

## Cost of inaction
Every bang passthrough or any inbound message whose harness turn ends without the question, permission, or failure hooks firing is a silent black hole with no signal either way; this already cost 6+ days of an unanswered thread on a real message while the underlying work was actually completed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A repro test exists that injects a message via the routes mechanism, simulates a pane resolving work without an explicit tg call, and asserts the user is notified or the gap is loudly surfaced (e.g. a stale-thread nudge) instead of silence.
- [ ] Either a Stop-success hook channel is added mirroring StopFailure's pattern in hook-install.ts that relays a summary back to the originating Telegram thread, or a documented watchdog/nudge mechanism exists and is wired into the daemon, for any turn that ends normally without hitting the AskUserQuestion, PermissionRequest, or StopFailure hooks.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links

## Skipped gates
- links: false positives: the Telegram message id and the file paths named in --what are not GitHub/PR references or repo links, they are plain narrative identifiers

title: Add offline dry-run validation for tg escalation-format gate
body:
## What

the escalation-format gate is deliberately strict by design, but the only way to test a candidate message today is a live send attempt against the human's real inbox
