title: pre-send-text decision-gate hook inspects pre-substitution shell text, blindspot for $(cat file) message bodies
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Root-caused 2026-07-23: the pre-send-text escalation-format gate hook (agent-tools decision_request_format.py, registered as a Claude Code pre-bash hook) reads the shell command text literally, before the shell resolves command substitution syntax. A well-formed decision-request message piped in via command substitution is therefore invisible to the hook -- it only ever sees the literal unexpanded substitution syntax, never the actual HTML/table content -- so it gets rejected as a bare question with no escalation structure even though the real message is fully compliant.

## User impact
Agents repeatedly and confusingly get blocked sending a well-formed message, waste escalation cycles retrying, and can end up sending test noise to the human's live Telegram channel while debugging the false rejection. This happened for real in this session on 2026-07-23: an agent drafted a compliant message, was rejected on about five consecutive attempts, initially misdiagnosed it as a content problem, sent noise to the live channel, and only found the real cause by reading the hook source directly. The workaround that worked was pasting the message body literally into the command instead of using command substitution.

## Cost of inaction
Recurs for every future agent that drafts a non-trivial decision-request via a prepared file plus command substitution, a completely standard shell pattern for passing prepared file content, so this will keep costing agents multiple failed attempts and risking live-channel noise indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A well-formed decision-request message passed via tg --format html --tag decision with the body supplied through command substitution (cat message.html) is NOT rejected as a bare question when message.html contains valid escalation structure (an HTML table or the required section markers).
- [ ] Either the pre-send-text decision-request-format hook is fixed to inspect the fully-resolved argv text tg actually receives instead of the raw pre-substitution command string, verified by a regression test that sends via command substitution and asserts it passes; or, if the hook is structurally a true pre-execution shell hook that can only ever see literal command text, tg's --help output and the decision-request-discipline skill are updated to explicitly document that command substitution must not be used to pass the message body, and that the body must be pasted literally into the tg argv instead.

title: No dry-run mode: agents testing the --tag decision|question gate leak placeholder content to the live chat
body:
## What

`tg` had no way to validate a `--tag decision|question` message's structural
compliance with the escalation-format gate without actually sending it. The
gate (features/cli/escalation-format.ts) is purely structural — it checks for
a table, pros/cons keywords, a recommendation, a file:line reference, and
Rich Message structure (headings/lists/hr). It cannot tell real content from
placeholder/scaffold text, so a structurally-valid-but-still-placeholder draft
passes it exactly like a real message would.

## Why (motivation)

Root-caused 2026-07-25 from the live outbound history log
(`~/.config/tg-cli/tg-ctl.8574086668.history.jsonl`, message_id 10192-10202):
an agent working on the HYP-1061 decision request iterated against the strict
gate by sending real messages to see whether they'd pass, since there was no
local/offline way to check. Two of those live sends (message_id 10199, 10200)
still carried the gate's own guidance-example scaffold text verbatim —
"foo bar baz test." for Context, Option A pros "ok" cons "bad", "foo.ts:1" for
"where to look" — because the structural check has no way to detect
placeholder content. Six live messages went out in under 90 seconds before the
real content (message_id 10201/10202) finally landed. The human (Alex)
received this as six confusing/garbled Telegram messages instead of one clean
decision request and had to ask "why did you send me 6 messages like that
instead of a real options message" (message_id 10204).

This is not a one-off: an earlier occurrence of the same class
(message_id 9936, an agent apologizing "sorry, this was a test message from
debugging the tg formatter, ignore foo.ts:42/Option A/B — those are
placeholders") shows this has already happened before without a durable fix.

## User impact

The human's live Telegram channel receives multiple noisy, sometimes-garbled
test messages whenever an agent needs to iterate against the strict
escalation-format gate — instead of one clean decision request. This directly
degrades trust in the escalation channel (a channel whose entire design intent
is "a clean, 30-second-readable request").

## Cost of inaction

Recurs every time an agent needs to draft a non-trivial `--tag decision` or
`--tag question` message and isn't confident it'll pass the gate on the first
try — which, given the gate's strictness (headings, hr dividers, lists,
pros/cons keywords, file:line ref, all required), is common. Each recurrence
costs several live messages of noise on the human's phone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `tg --dry-run [...]` validates/renders a message through every LOCAL
      guard (escalation-format gate, cjk/mixed-script guard, table/pipe-table
      conversion) and prints PASS/FAIL, but makes NO network call and
      requires NO TG_BOT_TOKEN/TG_CHAT_ID — proven with a mock Bot-API server
      that must receive zero requests for a `--dry-run` send, compliant or
      malformed.
- [x] A regression test reproduces the incident directly: the EXACT
      placeholder body from message_id 10199/10200 ("foo bar baz test." /
      Option A "ok"/"bad" / "foo.ts:1") passes `--dry-run` cleanly (0 requests
      received) — and, as a sanity check proving the harness is real, the same
      body WITHOUT `--dry-run` DOES reach the mock server.
- [x] `--help` documents `--dry-run`; the decision-request-discipline skill
      tells agents to self-check a draft with `tg --dry-run` instead of a real
      send.

## Screenshots

(none — CLI behavior change, not UI)

## Links

- Related, separate root cause already tracked: #238 (pre-send-text hook
  sees pre-substitution shell text, a different blind spot in the SAME class
  of "agent iterates against the escalation gate via real sends").

title: tg: dry-run/send guard parity is enforced by code position, not structure
body:
## What

`--dry-run` (added in #239 / PR TBD) works by short-circuiting the main
`if (import.meta.main)` block in `tg` right after the last local guard
(escalation-format, cjk/mixed-script, table/pipe-table conversion) and right
before the credential check + transport/send path. This is correct today,
but the guarantee "dry-run validates everything a real send would, minus the
network call" is enforced only by the LINE POSITION of that short-circuit in
a several-hundred-line linear script, documented in a comment.

## Why (motivation)

Review finding (Fable, on the --dry-run PR): any future guard added below
the short-circuit — or any reordering of the existing ones — silently exempts
itself from `--dry-run` with no test failure, because the tests can only
assert against guards that exist today. There is nothing structural (a type,
a single function both paths call) that would force a new guard to be dry-run
-aware.

## User impact

A future guard (e.g. a new content-safety check, a new attachment
constraint) could be added below the cutoff without anyone noticing it's
invisible to `--dry-run` — reintroducing exactly the failure class `--dry-run`
exists to prevent: an agent trusts a clean dry-run result, then the real send
fails or behaves differently for a reason dry-run never checked.

## Cost of inaction

Low probability per change, but the failure mode is silent (no test breaks)
and the blast radius is a repeat of the original incident this flag fixes
(tg-cli#239) — live-channel noise the agent didn't expect after a "passing"
dry-run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The validate-and-render pipeline (escalation-format gate, --table
      final check, cjk/mixed-script guard, pipe-table conversion) is
      extracted into a single function that both the `--dry-run` path and
      the real-send path call, so a new guard added to that function is
      automatically covered by both — parity by construction, not by
      keeping two code paths in sync by hand.
- [ ] A test proves the structural guarantee: e.g. a guard stub added to the
      shared function is exercised by both an integration test hitting
      `--dry-run` and one hitting a real send against the mock server.

## Links
- Depends on / follows: #239

title: tg --dry-run: fix attachment-detection ordering and add pre-autolink and rich-message validation
body:
## What
tg --dry-run currently short-circuits (in [features/cli/args.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/cli/args.ts) and tg's dry-run block) BEFORE two things the real send path does: (1) resolving auto-attached file:line references and large-fenced-block-to-document attachments (see [features/auto-attach/normalize.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/auto-attach/normalize.ts)), and (2) the final pre-autolink render plus rich-message preflight validation (see [features/auto-attach/transmitter.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/auto-attach/transmitter.ts)). Two High-severity findings came out of the extra review-quorum passes run to ship [PR #241](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/241) (recorded under review task code labeled TG dash 241, model codex gpt-5.6-sol, 2026-07-28): (a) an auto-attachable file:line reference or a large fenced code block in the body dry-runs as a plain-text OK, while a real send would actually create and attach a document, a misleading partial pass; (b) dry-run reports the body well formed and OK before the canonical final render and rich-message length and format preflight run, so an oversized or malformed rich body can pass dry-run but then get rejected or mis-rendered on the real send.

## Why (motivation)
Pre-existing gap in the --dry-run feature shipped in [PR #241](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/241). Surfaced during the extra review-quorum passes run to satisfy gh ship's review-quorum gate for that PR, not caused by the PR's rebase itself, a real correctness gap in the feature it shipped.

## User impact
An agent using --dry-run to self-check a decision or question draft before a real send can get a false OK for a body that would actually attach an unexpected document, or that the real send would reject or mis-render as an oversized rich message, defeating the exact purpose --dry-run was built for (see [PR #241](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/241), filed against [#239](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/239)).

## Cost of inaction
The false-confidence gap stays open: an agent trusts the OK from --dry-run, sends for real, and gets either an unexpected attachment or a rejected or garbled rich message in the live chat, the same class of incident --dry-run was built to prevent (see [PR #241](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/241)'s incident writeup, message ids 10192 through 10202).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tg --dry-run on a body containing an auto-attachable file:line reference or a large fenced code block (over 1024 chars) reports the same attachment outcome (document created and attached) that a real send would produce, not a silent text-only OK.
- [ ] tg --dry-run runs the message through the same final pre-autolink render and rich-message length and format preflight the real send path uses, so a body that a real send would reject or mis-render is reported as failing under --dry-run too. Add regression tests for a rich body over the length limit and for a title-only dry-run producing an empty rendered body.

title: Escalation gate hasWallOfText measures RAW line length incl. HTML markup — any single-line HTML body >350 chars is deny-by-default blocked
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
features/cli/escalation-format.ts hasWallOfText() splits the body on newlines and flags any non-markup line longer than WALL_LINE_CHARS (350). But agents emit the decision-request HTML as ONE single line (no newlines). The markup-skip regex only skips lines STARTING with table/ul/li tags, so a one-line body starting with <h3> is measured in full: any well-structured decision message longer than 350 chars fails the readability check and is deny-by-default blocked. Verified via tg --dry-run on 2026-08-01: the gate's own documented template (just under 350 chars) passes; adding ONE more short <li> ('B — also fine') pushes it over and fails with the misleading 'break run-on paragraphs' complaint. The check was designed for multi-line prose bodies (tg#8970), not single-line HTML.

> **tg#8970** — Alex, 2026-07-16 17:05 UTC: За исключением таблицы это сообщение это стена текста без структуры. Очень тяжело читается. Подумай как такого избегать…
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:8970 -->

## User impact
Every real decision/question escalation with 2+ recommendation bullets or 2+ evidence links is hard-blocked, forcing agents to either mangle the message to fit 350 chars or bypass with ESCALATION_GATE_ENFORCE=0 — which is exactly the bypass-training the gate exists to prevent.

## Cost of inaction
Agents learn to route around the gate; structured escalations get silently degraded to plain messages or blocked mid-report (this already happened live during the conloca HYP-1162 report).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] hasWallOfText strips HTML markup before measuring, or measures per-text-node rather than per raw line, so a structured single-line HTML body of any length passes
- [ ] Regression test: a single-line HTML body with h3/table/ul(3+ li)/hr sections and >350 chars validates OK
- [ ] A genuine wall-of-text (single prose paragraph >350 chars, no markup) still fails

## Screenshots

title: tg --dry-run gate gives different accept/reject verdict than real send for byte-identical content depending on shell arg-passing mechanism
body:
## What
Reproduce and fix the divergence between tg --dry-run and a real tg send for byte-identical --tag decision/question HTML bodies. Passing the body via $(cat file) (command substitution reading a file) or via a shell variable ("$C") makes the --dry-run structural gate ([escalationFormatGate](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/cli/args.ts#L270-L293), calling [validateEscalationFormat](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/cli/escalation-format.ts#L96-L143)) reject it as a 'bare question, no structure' failure. Passing the exact same bytes as a direct literal string argument on the tg command line makes the SAME gate accept it. Both dry-run and a real send run through the identical parse -> [decodeTextEscapes](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/cli/text-escapes.ts#L9-L16) -> escalationFormatGate pipeline ([tg#L929-L934](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/tg#L929-L934) and [tg#L1013-L1045](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/tg#L1013-L1045)), so per the code the verdict should depend only on caption bytes, not on how the shell delivered the argv entry. Needs someone to reproduce both ways side by side (tg --dry-run --tag decision --format html "$(cat f.html)" vs tg --dry-run --tag decision --format html "$LITERAL_SAME_TEXT") and diff exactly what argv/caption the gate receives in each case (byte dump, not eyeballing) to find where the divergence is introduced.

## Why (motivation)
Hit while drafting a decision-request message with tg --format html --tag decision during the pre-send self-check recommended by this repo's decision-request-discipline skill: tg --dry-run --tag decision --format html "$(cat file)" and "$C" (shell variable) were rejected with a bare-question / no-structure failure, but the exact same bytes passed as a literal string argument on the tg command line were accepted by the same gate.

## User impact
The person the agent is asking to decide something over Telegram (the CTO) is the one who ends up affected: either they never get asked because the agent gave up after a confusing false rejection from a check that was supposed to just be a local sanity check, or they DO get a badly-formatted message on their phone because a false pass fooled the agent into thinking the safety check had approved it. Either way the human can no longer trust that 'dry-run said OK' means the real message will actually look right.

## Cost of inaction
Agents keep hitting confusing gate rejections when composing longer HTML from a file (the natural way to draft multi-hundred-char structured decision/question messages) and either abandon --dry-run entirely (losing the safety check) or waste real sends on the live human channel debugging the gate instead of the message content.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tg --dry-run and a real tg send agree on accept/reject for byte-identical HTML --tag decision/question content regardless of whether the argument arrives via a literal string, $(cat file), or a shell variable.
- [ ] A regression test captures the specific repro (same HTML bytes passed via $(cat file) and via a shell variable both produce the same dry-run verdict as the literal-argument form) so this cannot silently regress.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body:
Related data point on the same gate, different angle: this time the send was **not** the file/variable-substitution path this issue already tracks -- it was passed as a literal argument on the command line, which is the "safe" path documented elsewhere in this thread. Repro: - `tg --tag decision --format html ""` - Content was well-formed HTML matching the gate's own expected decision-request template almost exactly: `

Context

...

Options

...pros/cons...

Recommendation

...

Where to look

...` - Rejected, with the generic message that echoes the gate's own placeholder example back: `Blocked: --tag decision|question must follow the decision-request format.` - Reproduced twice in a row with the same content and the same literal-argument passing mode -- not a one-off flake. - Also tried the documented override env var `RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_DECISION_REQUEST_FORMAT=""` to bypass the block. It did **not** bypass it -- the same rejection reappeared. - Falling back to `--tag report` with the identical HTML content sent successfully with no changes to the body. So on top of the file/variable-substitution vs. literal-argument disagreement already tracked here, we now also have: literal-argument content that matches the gate's own template is still rejected, and the documented override flag does not unblock it either. Filing as a comment here rather than a new issue since this looks like the same gate misbehaving, just a different angle on the same underlying bug.

title: Verify escalation-format gate Readability check against real decision-request content (reported false-rejects)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A subagent reported (relayed by Alex via Telegram tg#11788) that --tag question's escalation-format gate 'Readability' sub-check only accepts the tool's own toy template and rejects realistic decision-request content: real file paths, multi-row option tables, and multi-item recommendation lists all allegedly fail, while the literal template text (and single-word edits to it) passes.

> **tg#11788** — Alex, 2026-08-17 10:35 UTC: 2 заведи и починим
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:11788 -->

## User impact
If the gate really is this strict, whenever an agent needs to ask Alex a real yes/no decision through tg --tag question, the tool refuses to send it and the agent has to either keep rewording a real question until it looks like the tool's toy example, or turn the safety check off entirely — either way Alex either doesn't get asked, or gets asked without the structure that would let him decide in 30 seconds.

## Cost of inaction
The claim stays unverified folklore: either a real usability bug keeps blocking every real escalation to Alex, or (as my own independent testing already found) the gate already works fine and nobody records that — leaving both Alex and future agents unsure whether --tag question is safe to use, with zero regression protection against a future change quietly reintroducing false-rejects.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Re-run the exact reported failure probes (a real >=40-char file path like [.github/workflows/self-hosted-runner-smoke.yml](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/.github/workflows/self-hosted-runner-smoke.yml):1, a 3-row Options table with 2-word cells, a 2-item Recommendation list, Context lines at ~26 vs ~28 chars) via 'tg --tag question --dry-run' against [features/cli/escalation-format.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/cli/escalation-format.ts) on main, with command+output captured as evidence.
- [ ] If any probe genuinely fails, fix the specific broken check with the smallest change (do not disable/water down the gate) and prove the fix with a before/after dry-run.
- [ ] Add regression tests in [tests/escalation-format.test.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/tests/escalation-format.test.ts) for the exact probe shapes (real file path, 3-row table, 2-item list) asserting the correct (pass) outcome, so a future threshold/regex edit cannot silently re-break real escalations without failing CI.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body:
## Investigation result Root cause found and fixed in PR #262. **What did NOT reproduce**: I re-ran ~15 more `tg --tag question --dry-run` probes against `features/cli/escalation-format.ts` on `main`, mirroring every specific claim in the original report (real file path, 3-row table, 2-item recommendation list, Context line length ~26 vs ~28 chars). None of them failed when the body used real literal newlines between sections (`--tag question --dry-run "

...

\n

...`). All of those claims are pinned as passing regression tests in the PR. **What DID reproduce, and is the real bug**: when the exact same structurally-valid body is composed as ONE continuous string with no literal `\n` between sections (very plausible if an agent builds the `tg` argument without explicit newlines), `hasWallOfText` in `features/cli/escalation-format.ts` split on literal `\n` only. The whole one-line body becomes a single "line" for the length check, and its raw character count trivially exceeds the 350-char `WALL_LINE_CHARS` threshold once the content is realistic (the toy template as one line is 345 chars — just under; the same shape with one real filename swapped in is 538). This produces exactly the reported pattern: template passes, any real content fails, "regardless of wording." Fixed by making `hasWallOfText` scan "visual lines" (a virtual break before each opening block tag, after each closing/void one) instead of literal-`\n` lines, so the verdict no longer depends on the caller's newline formatting choice. See PR #262 for the full diff, review trail (2 real regressions caught and fixed in the first-draft fix before it shipped), and test coverage.

title: harness-event mislabels bare StopFailure notifications with stale tmux window name instead of live harness kind
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
tg-ctl's installed Claude Code StopFailure hook runs bare (tg-ctl harness-event, no --agent flag, per hook-install.ts line 277). Its fallback agent-label resolver, resolveAgentForPane (tg-ctl lines 3699-3702), read the windowName field (the tmux window's static, user-set label) instead of the agent field (the live process-tree-detected harness kind) from listAgentCandidates -- even though that function computes both fields, and a parallel sibling function already correctly uses windowName for its own distinct purpose. Looks like a copy-paste bug.

## User impact
When Claude Code hits a rate limit or crashes, the operator gets a Telegram alert naming which coding-agent session needs attention. Sometimes that alert names the wrong agent entirely (says codex when the session is actually claude code), so the operator can waste time looking in the wrong terminal window or dismissing a real alert as noise.

## Cost of inaction
Operators keep getting misleading agent attribution in critical rate-limit and crash alerts, making it harder to know which actual session needs attention.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A hermetic regression test (fake tmux and ps on PATH) proves: a pane whose tmux window is named 'codex' but whose live process is 'claude' produces a StopFailure notification correctly labeled 'claude', not 'codex'.
- [ ] The full test suite (bun test ./tests) has zero new failures compared to the pre-fix baseline.

title: harness-event bare StopFailure alerts lose per-pane identity when multiple panes run the same harness
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Follow-up from [ticket #263](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/263), which fixed the agent-kind mislabeling bug. Two independent review models flagged the same tradeoff on that fix: buildLimitNotification's head line renders only the harness kind (e.g. claude), not which specific pane or window. The prior (buggy) window-name-based label accidentally gave rough per-session disambiguation; the fixed version has several panes running the same harness render an identical alert head, e.g. two claude sessions both say the exact same 'claude hit its session limit' with no way to tell which one from the headline alone. windowName is already resolved separately in runHarnessEventPayload (tg-ctl around line 3722) so the data is available, just not carried into the notification text.

## User impact
An operator running several coding-agent sessions of the same kind (for example three claude code windows on different repos) gets a rate-limit or crash alert in Telegram that only says which kind of agent failed, not which specific window or project -- so they have to check every open session by hand to find the one that actually stopped.

## Cost of inaction
Operators with multiple same-harness sessions keep losing time hunting for which session actually triggered a critical alert, especially under load when several sessions are running at once.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Design decision made and documented: either the StopFailure notification text carries both the harness kind and the window name (e.g. 'claude in gitapp'), or an explicit reasoning for why harness kind alone is sufficient.
- [ ] If implemented: a regression test proves that two panes running the same harness kind (e.g. two claude sessions in different windows) produce distinguishable StopFailure notification text.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body: Implementation note from code review on #263: `resolveAgentForPane` and `resolveWindowNameForPane` each call `listAgentCandidates()` independently, taking separate tmux/ps snapshots. That's harmless redundancy today (each resolver reads only its own field), but whoever implements this ticket by combining window name + agent kind into one notification should resolve the candidate ONCE per event and read both fields off that single record -- otherwise a pane reused mid-event (the exact premise of #263) could pair one snapshot's window name with a different snapshot's detected agent kind.

title: limit-continue arm/fire guard recovers agent from windowName, same drift weakness as the harness-event bug
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Found during code review of [ticket #263](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/263) (fixed a different bare-hook resolver reading the tmux window name instead of the live-detected harness). handleLimitContinue recovers its agent value from .windowName (tg-ctl around line 6803) and fireAutoContinue skips when live.windowName does not match the stored value (tg-ctl around line 6770) -- the same class of static-label-used-as-live-identity that #263 fixed elsewhere, but pre-existing and NOT touched by that fix. A window renamed between the tap and the fire could falsely skip a legitimate auto-continue, and a same-named window that now hosts a different harness still passes the guard since only pane liveness is checked, not harness identity.

## User impact
An operator who taps the auto-continue button on a rate-limit alert can have the retry silently fail to fire if the tmux window got renamed in the meantime (for example by tg-ctl's own topic-bind renaming), with no visible error explaining why the continue never happened.

## Cost of inaction
The auto-continue feature keeps a subtle failure mode where a legitimate retry silently never fires, and nothing in the product surfaces why -- the same class of confusing, hard-to-diagnose bug as the one just fixed in #263.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Design decision documented: whether handleLimitContinue and fireAutoContinue should key on live-detected harness kind instead of windowName, or whether windowName is intentionally correct there as a pane-identity proxy (distinct from the harness-kind question #263 fixed).
- [ ] If changed: a regression test proves the auto-continue guard still fires correctly when a window is renamed between the tap and the fire, and correctly skips when the pane now hosts a different harness under the same window name.

title: Late-deliver a Telegram permission tap by injecting the digit into the still-showing terminal menu
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
CTO spec, verbatim: 'no waiting process — check via tmux whether the permission request is still showing, and send the keypresses.' The prior behavior (tg-cli#31/#98) only queued a late tap for delivery on hook RECONNECT, but a terminal-fallback permission may never get a fresh hook to reconnect, so the queued tap could wait forever despite the human having already answered

## User impact
A tapped Approve/Reject on a timed-out permission request now actually reaches the agent's terminal immediately instead of silently sitting queued with no guarantee of ever being delivered

## Cost of inaction
Users keep hitting the reported bug: 'queued Approve for rig -- delivered automatically once the hook reconnects' when in practice no reconnect ever comes, so the tapped decision is effectively lost and the human must go answer in the terminal anyway

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A tap on Approve/Reject after a permission's hook socket closed re-checks the pane via tmux capture-pane, and if Claude Code's numbered menu is still showing, injects the matching digit directly instead of only queuing for a hook reconnect
- [ ] When the menu is no longer showing (already resolved, not yet fallen back to terminal, or a non-claude agent), the existing queue-and-wait-for-reconnect behavior is unchanged — no regression
- [ ] The digit-submits-without-Enter behavior is verified live against a real Claude Code instance (not assumed) before landing

title: tg-ctl permission pane-inject: deferred hardening (verbose deny label, state-machine extraction, other prompt shapes, deny-window guard test)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Filed while landing tg-ctl#267 (pane-inject late-delivery for permissions) — 3 rounds of multi-model review surfaced these as legitimate but lower-priority/non-blocking findings: the deny label and other-prompt-shapes items are unverified assumptions that fail SAFE (fall through to the existing queue-and-wait path) rather than fail dangerously, and the state-machine extraction is a design improvement, not a correctness bug

## User impact
A person who taps Reject (deny) on a Telegram permission card, or who is approving an edit/write/plan-approval prompt rather than a Bash command, does not yet get the instant pane-delivery speed-up this feature promises — their tap still falls back to the slower queue-and-wait path, the same experience as before this feature existed. Nobody gets a WORSE or wrong outcome from this gap, just a missed speed-up for those specific cases

## Cost of inaction
The pane-inject feature stays narrower than it could be (still safe, just less useful for deny/other tools), and the inline claim/rollback logic stays harder to reason about for future changes in that area

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Live-verify Claude Code's actual rendered deny-option label (currently assumed exact 'No'); if it's ever a verbose form like 'No, and tell Claude what to do differently', decide whether to prefix-match deny (safe, since any 'No, ...' is still a refusal) and implement it
- [ ] Live-test claude's edit/write-tool permission prompts and plan-approval ('Would you like to proceed?') — confirm their marker text/option wording, extend permission-menu.ts's PROCEED_MARKER/option matching if they differ from the Bash-permission shape already verified
- [ ] Consider extracting the claim/verify/rollback state machine (tg-ctl's ~90-line inline block in the permission branch of lateDeliverAbandonedQuestion) into features/tg-ctl/questions.ts or a small dedicated helper with an explicit state-transition API, instead of inline map surgery in runDaemon
- [ ] Add an integration test for the shouldDeferInbound guard on the pane-inject path (a live pending question on the same pane must fall through to queuing, not attempt injection)

comments.body:
Two more findings from round 2 of tg-cli#267's review gate (after the `hasLiveCursor` fix landed), both non-blocking and fail-safe on the approval axis — adding here rather than blocking #267 further:

**1. Duplicate live card on daemon-restart race.** Pane-delivered permissions are recorded in `answeredButtons` with `delivery: "pane"`, but the reconnect/replay guard in `handleHookSocketLine` (kind-guarded to `question` today) doesn't read them. If the daemon restarts while the `tg-ctl ask` client is still alive, gets restored to `abandonedButtons`, and a human taps → pane-inject succeeds before the client reconnects, a subsequent reconnect resend can post a **second, duplicate live card** for an already-decided permission — a tap on it answers a socket Claude Code no longer reads, while the toast still claims success. The questions path already has an `already-pane-delivered` branch for exactly this shape; permissions pane-delivery needs the same handling.

**2. Third unmodeled resolve variant: cursor retained on a resolved menu.** The post-inject confirm now handles "text vanishes" and "text retained, cursor stripped" (the `hasLiveCursor` fix). The one remaining unverified possibility — Claude Code leaves the resolved box in scrollback WITH `❯` still on it — isn't modeled. In that world a successful delivery would read as "still pending" (queues a decision that already took effect), and the PRE-inject gate would also stay satisfied, so a stale tap against old scrollback could inject a bare digit into whatever's currently focused. Fail-safe on approval (never grants something un-approved), but worth resolving via a live capture the next time someone verifies the other open questions here (deny label, edit/write/plan-approval shapes).

Both found via multi-model review (Opus + k3), not yet independently live-verified.

Round 3 findings (after the log-reason fix), consolidated:

**Reentrancy during the 400ms confirm window — checked, NOT a bug.** Both Opus and GLM independently flagged a hypothetical double-inject if a second tap for the same requestId arrives while the first is mid-confirm. Verified against the actual dispatch code: `for (const action of step.actions) { lastActionOk = await executeAction(action) }` (tg-ctl:7742-7743) is explicitly documented as "STRICTLY SEQUENTIAL — one action fully completes... before the next starts. ... do NOT make action dispatch concurrent." This matches round 2's k3 review, which already verified the same thing independently. No fix needed; noting here so a future reader doesn't re-litigate it without checking the dispatch loop first.

**Worth tracking (adding to this ticket's scope, not fixing now):**
- `capturePane()` uses `Bun.spawnSync` with no timeout, called synchronously from the async daemon path — a wedged/contended tmux server blocks the ENTIRE daemon (Telegram polling, hook-socket reads, all timers) for as long as the subprocess hangs. Should be async (`Bun.spawn` piped, or bounded with a timeout/killSignal) — medium severity, this one's a real robustness gap, not just theoretical.
- `hasLiveCursor` is keyed on the literal `❯` glyph with no fallback signal — if a Claude Code version/theme ever renders differently, the whole feature silently stops firing (fail-soft, but invisible without checking `no-live-cursor` logs).
- Line-exact identity matching doesn't account for Claude Code possibly truncating long commands in the permission box itself (only hook-side truncation is handled) — exactly the long-running-command population this feature targets could be under-served.
- Missing unit test: a plan-approval pane fed to `parsePermissionMenu` should return null (safety currently rests on the marker text differing, unpinned).
- Missing integration test: `shouldDeferInbound` guard on the permission pane-inject path specifically (a live second question on the same pane must fall through to queuing).
- Minor: the truncated-identity prefix branch in `permissionMenuMatchesRequest` is effectively dead — `summarizeInput`'s real truncation is mid-word, but the branch requires a word-boundary-ending prefix, so it never matches in practice. Either drop the boundary requirement or document the branch as queue-always.

All non-blocking, fail-safe on the approval axis (worst case is a missed speed-up, never a wrong action).

title: escalation-format: withVisualLineBreaks is markup-context-blind (breaks inside <pre>/<code>) and its block-tag set is incomplete
body:
Follow-up from review of PR #262 (fix/escalation-gate-readability-verify), which fixed the tg-cli#261 newline-formatting bug for the reported cases. Two related, lower-severity gaps were found during that PR's review but are architectural, not the originally reported bug, and were deliberately deferred rather than folded into that fix: ## 1. `withVisualLineBreaks` splits inside `
`/`` content — false positive

`OPEN_BLOCK_RE`/`CLOSE_BLOCK_RE` in `features/cli/escalation-format.ts` are markup-context-blind: they break on tag-shaped *text* inside a code block, not just real markup. A body with a `
` line containing an HTML example as literal text (e.g. `
renders as "
" + ...400 chars...
`) regresses: pre-fix, the line started with `` gets a virtual break injected, splitting the code block, and the tail (400 chars of code) gets flagged as a wall of text / counted as Context prose.

Fix direction: strip or mask `
`/`` span contents before running `withVisualLineBreaks`, or compute line length on tag-stripped text. Needs a regression test: a long `
` line containing `
`-shaped text.

## 2. Block-tag break/skip sets are incomplete for Telegram's Rich Message tier

`
`, `
`, ``, ``, `` are block-level in Telegram Rich Messages (per this repo's own AGENTS.md) but are in neither `OPEN_BLOCK_RE`/`CLOSE_BLOCK_RE` nor the skip-lists. A one-line body using these tags still gets a newline-format-dependent verdict — the tg-cli#261 bug class survives for this tag subset. Fix is two-sided: adding a tag to the break set without also adding it to both skip-lists trades one false verdict for another.

Both were verified via `review diff` (k3/kimi-code) during PR #262 and are edge cases (unusual input shapes), not reproductions of a live reported bug — hence tracked here instead of blocking that PR.

title: tg-ctl: no-reply anchor uses the CTO's own last message, not any agent's last outbound send
body:
## What

Live incident: Alex sent a non-reply message right after ext-cc sent him an inbound message, and it misrouted to ext-cc's session instead of the one he intended. title: tg-ctl anchor: centralize recordLastAlexTarget at a delivery chokepoint + close remaining gaps
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
PR #271 (tg-ctl no-reply anchor fix, closes the live ext-cc misroute incident) went through 5 rounds of multi-model review. The core correctness bugs (pane-ID reuse, explicit-routing gaps for picker-tap/reply/agent/media-caption, cwd-required schema) were all fixed and merged. These remaining items are architecture-quality/coverage findings from round 5 (Fable-architect + Opus + k3), left as a scoped follow-up rather than expanding an already-large diff further.

## User impact
Without centralizing the recording responsibility, each NEW routing feature is a fresh bet that the author remembers to call recordLastAlexTarget — exactly the class of bug this PR fixed 4 times over across review rounds

## Cost of inaction
The anchor mechanism keeps accumulating scattered call sites, and a future routing feature silently reintroduces a milder version of the original misroute bug

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] recordLastAlexTarget is called from ONE wrapper around confirmed delivery (executeInjectSteps success / enqueueDeferred), not hand-called at 7+ scattered call sites, so a new routing path gets anchor semantics automatically instead of by review finding
- [ ] Topic-routed delivery either also records the anchor, or the module docstring's 'no staleness by design' rationale is corrected to state the anchor only reflects non-topic activity
- [ ] Missing regression tests added: named /agent <name> <msg> path records the anchor, the armed one-shot route records it, the media-caption path records it, a failed inject does NOT move the anchor, and anchor-pane-gone falls back to the picker
- [ ] Anchor filename in tests is derived via ctlPaths(...) instead of a hardcoded 'tg-ctl.123.last-alex-target.json' string literal, so a naming-scheme drift fails the test loudly instead of passing vacuously
- [ ] A deferred (queued-behind-a-question) inbound message whose flush later fails or never happens does not leave a stale anchor recorded at enqueue time — updated only after injectDeferredOne confirms delivery, with a regression test for a stuck/failed flush (round-3 codex finding).
- [ ] A failed unlinkSync in invalidateLastAlexTarget is made observable (logged), so a broken invalidation is visible in daemon.log rather than silent (round-3 codex finding).
- [ ] Round-5 codex findings (now fixed in code, tests still missing): bare /agent <message> single-candidate route and unrecognized-reply single-candidate route both now call recordLastAlexTarget after confirmed delivery — add dedicated integration tests for each (mirroring the existing 'ORDINARY auto-bound delivery records the anchor' pattern).
- [ ] Round-7 codex P1: the anchor is a single per-bot file with no sender scoping, but control.allowed_senders lets OTHER Telegram users message through the same bot — their deliveries currently overwrite the SAME anchor the CTO's own routing depends on. Scope the anchor to the primary owner (chatId) specifically, ideally as part of the single delivery-chokepoint refactor above (gate recording on sender identity there), with a regression test using an allowed extra sender targeting a different pane. Not reachable today with the default empty allowed_senders config, but a real gap once that list is non-empty.
- [ ] Round-7 Opus: a pathless-tmux pane (live panePath empty) can never record or resolve the anchor at all — fail-closed/safe but a real capability regression vs. the removed lastMessagePane fallback for that configuration. Consider a record-side fallback to the pane's REGISTRATION cwd when the live panePath is empty (the resolve-side reuse guard genuinely needs a live path, so that side stays as-is).

(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: internal review-round citations (Fable/Opus/k3 findings), not GitHub URLs

title: tg-ctl: last-alex-target anchor edge cases deferred from tg-cli#78 follow-up review
body:

## Why (motivation)

title: tg-ctl: the live daemon process never restarts after a merge, so shipped fixes silently sit inert for weeks
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Discovered while fixing [issue #274](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/274): the live daemon (pid 9484) had been running continuously since 2026-07-30 without a single restart, while main advanced 8+ commits (2026-07-30 through 2026-08-19) including at least one other user-facing fix ([PR #247](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/247), omp branding). None of those fixes were actually active in Alex's real session the whole time, even though they were merged and the checked-out code on disk was updated (bun does not hot-reload a running script)

## User impact
Alex ships a fix, sees it merged, and reasonably assumes it is now working — but until something happens to restart the daemon (a crash, a manual tg-ctl restart, a reboot), he is still running the OLD behavior and won't know it. This is exactly what caused the original agent-route id-tag bug (linked above) to look confusing: the bug felt worse/different than expected because weeks of other unrelated fixes were also silently inactive

## Cost of inaction
Every future tg-ctl fix carries the same silent risk: merged does not mean deployed, and there is currently no signal telling Alex or an agent that the running process is stale relative to main

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] There is a documented or automated way to know the running tg-ctl daemon's pid start-time is at or after the live checkout's current git commit time, so a stale-daemon situation is detectable (e.g. tg-ctl status prints a warning when the daemon's start time predates the checked-out commit's date)
- [ ] There is a repeatable, documented step (a git post-merge hook, a periodic restart, or an explicit step in the standard tg-cli workflow) that restarts the daemon after main advances, so a merged fix takes effect within a bounded time instead of only on the next incidental restart

title: tg-ctl inbound Telegram albums (media_group_id) are split into separate per-photo deliveries instead of one bundled message
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex reported (2026-08-25) sending a 2-photo album with one text caption and receiving it as two separate deliveries: '[TG from Alex tg#13106] sent photo: .../599470604.jpg' with the caption attached, then a second, separate '[TG from Alex tg#13107] sent photo: .../599470605.jpg' with no text. Root cause confirmed by direct grep: zero references to media_group_id or mediaGroupId exist anywhere in the tg-cli codebase (features/tg-ctl/updates.ts's stepUpdates emits one photoAction per m.photo message with no grouping at all) -- this is a complete, not partial, gap.

> **tg#13106** — Alex, 2026-08-25 07:14 UTC: /agent rig А еще до сих пор поломано нажатие на кнопки при запросах на права и тп Я нажал а ничего не произошло
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:13106 -->
> **tg#13107** — Alex, 2026-08-25 07:14 UTC: [photo]
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:13107 -->

## User impact
An agent receiving a multi-photo report (e.g. two screenshots explaining one bug) sees them as two unrelated, uncaptioned-or-partially-captioned messages instead of one coherent bundle, making it harder to correctly associate images with their explanation

## Cost of inaction
Every future multi-photo album from Alex keeps arriving fragmented, and any caption on the album is attached to only ONE of the photos (whichever Telegram happens to send first), so an agent reading the SECOND photo's delivery sees no caption at all and has to infer context from the earlier message

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An inbound Telegram album (2+ photos sharing the same media_group_id, one caption on the first item) is delivered to the agent pane as ONE combined inbound event carrying all photo paths plus the single caption, not N separate '[TG from X] sent photo: ...' deliveries
- [ ] A regression test proves: 2 photos + 1 caption sent as a real Telegram album (same media_group_id across 2 separate getUpdates batches, arriving ~200-800ms ap,art) produce exactly one action/delivery, not two

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: no external reference beyond the tg session where Alex reported this; not a GitHub URL

comments.body:
Implementation sketch, from investigation (not yet built):

- `features/tg-ctl/updates.ts`'s `stepUpdates` (line ~441, `m.photo?.length` branch calling `photoAction`) is a PURE per-batch function — it has no state across polls. A real album's sibling photos can arrive in a LATER `getUpdates` batch (a different `stepUpdates` call a poll cycle later), so grouping cannot live inside this pure function alone.
- The daemon's main poll loop (`tg-ctl`, single call site at line ~7812: `const step = stepUpdates(json.result, {...})`) is where persistent, cross-poll state already lives for comparable buffering needs (e.g. `pendingAgent` — a `Map` with per-entry `timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>`, tg-ctl ~line 4141). A `pendingMediaGroups: Map<string /* media_group_id */, { photos: PhotoRef[]; caption?: string; from: string; timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> }>` following the same shape would fit the existing pattern.
- Flow: `stepUpdates` (or a thin wrapper around it) detects `m.media_group_id` on a photo message, buffers it into `pendingMediaGroups` instead of emitting a `photoAction` immediately, (re)arms a short debounce timer (~1-1.5s — Telegram album siblings arrive within ~1s of each other in practice), and on timer fire (or when a later poll's batch contains no new item for that group), flushes ONE combined action carrying all buffered photo refs + whichever item had a caption (usually the first, but don't assume — check every item, Telegram doesn't guarantee position).
- Delivery/injection side needs a bundled-photos action kind + inject text shape (currently `photoAction` produces one `mediaKind: 'photo'` action per photo, ~line 647-662) — likely a new `mediaKind: 'photo-group'` action carrying an array, or N photo actions that share one synthetic "group delivered" ack rather than N separate acks/deliveries.
- Test with a MOCK Telegram that returns the album's items split across TWO separate `getUpdates` responses (not one), since that's the realistic wire behavior — a test that puts both items in the same batch would pass without proving the actual cross-poll buffering works.

title: permission-menu.ts: multi-line Bash command matching for late-delivery pane-injection needs live-verified redesign (tg-cli#182 leg-2 follow-up)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A 3-round review (task 182, review diff --staged) attempted this exact fix and caught two real, escalating security findings each round: round 2 (Opus) -- an unanchored contiguous-run search let a shorter stale multi-line identity match as a line-prefix of a longer different live command, approving content the human never saw; round 3 (Codex) -- even after block-anchoring by exact line-count, the search still accepted a match against ANY block in the 12-line context, not specifically the one belonging to the current live menu, so an older leftover multi-line command still in view could get approved instead of the real live one; round 3 (Opus) also raised fundamental doubt whether the block-anchoring assumption (blank-line-delimited blocks) matches real Claude Code rendering for multi-line commands at all, since (unlike the single-line case, live-verified 2026-08-18) no live capture of an actual multi-line permission prompt was available to confirm it. Given the residual risk and unresolved verification gap, the fix was reverted rather than shipped under continued doubt on security-sensitive matching logic.

## User impact
A multi-line Bash permission prompt (heredocs, or a multi-step cleanup command written across several lines -- common for kill/sleep/rm-style scripts) can never be answered via the fast pane-injection path (tg-cli#267) and always falls into the queue-and-wait-for-hook-reconnect path, which then never resolves for a terminal-fallback permission (nothing causes a fresh hook to fire) -- confirmed by a real live incident 2026-08-25 where exactly this happened to a real agent session

## Cost of inaction
Every future multi-line permission prompt keeps silently stranding in queue-and-wait with no way to resolve via Telegram, forcing the human to notice and answer directly in the terminal every time -- the same friction tg-cli#267 already solved for single-line commands remains unsolved for multi-line ones

- [ ] permissionMenuMatchesRequest correctly and SAFELY matches a multi-line command identity (e.g. a 3-line pkill/sleep/rm-rf cleanup script) against a live tmux-captured Claude Code permission menu, verified against a REAL tmux capture-pane output from an actual multi-line Bash permission prompt (not a hand-written test fixture) -- confirming whether Claude Code renders a trailing description line after a multi-line command the same way it does for single-line ones

title: escalation-format gate rejects its own documented --tag decision example
body:
## What ## Why (motivation) hasContextProse() (features/cli/escalation-format.ts, lines 99-118) counts alphanumeric characters per VISUAL LINE after withVisualLineBreaks() splits the body at block-tag boundaries. A short context sentence wrapped as

Context

foo.ts:42 does X.

gets split into two separate lines ('

Context

' and '

foo.ts:42 does X.

'), each under the 20-alphanumeric-character threshold on its own (11 and 14 respectively), even though combined they clearly read as one real context sentence. Reproduced live: piping escalationFormatMessage's own printed GOOD example verbatim into 'tg --dry-run --tag decision --format html' fails with 'Missing: Context - a sentence of prose...', while the identical text passes instantly under --tag report (which skips validation entirely, confirming the content itself is fine). ## User impact Every agent that tries to follow the documented decision-request format for a genuinely short, terse Context line gets blocked by the gate meant to enforce that exact format, and has no path forward except silently downgrading the tag to 'report' (losing the escalation's distinct handling, such as the orange DECISION pill and whatever downstream handling depends on the tag) or using the ESCALATION_GATE_ENFORCE=0 escape hatch documented for 'genuine non-escalation / urgent edge case ONLY' -- neither is the intended fix for a message that is actually already well-formed. ## Cost of inaction Agents will keep silently mislabeling real decision requests as plain reports (or reaching for the escape hatch) whenever their Context sentence happens to be short, undermining the whole point of the decision/question tag distinction the skill and the gate exist to enforce. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] tg --dry-run --tag decision --format html with the exact GOOD example from 'tg help format' (the one printed in escalation-format.ts's own escalationFormatMessage template) exits 0, not 1 - [ ] hasContextProse() recognizes a Context sentence split across adjacent block-level tags (e.g.

Context

...

) as one unit, not two independently-scored fragments ## Screenshots (none) ## Links - (none) ## Skipped gates - links: internal source file reference (escalation-format.ts), not an external entity link

title: tg-ctl: scheduled usage report silently lost if machine asleep or off across the weekly/monthly boundary
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
usage-schedule.ts fires a check daily at 23:50 and only sends when today IS the exact boundary day (isEndOfWeek or isEndOfMonth). launchd runs a missed StartCalendarInterval job once on wake, at wake time, not the missed time, so if the machine is asleep or off at 23:50 on the boundary day, the check runs later on a non-boundary day and silently no-ops forever for that period.

## User impact
A user who enabled the scheduled push (see [PR #292](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/292)) can go an entire week or month with no usage report and no indication anything was missed, defeating the purpose of the automatic push.

## Cost of inaction
The scheduled feature is unreliable specifically for laptops that sleep overnight, the most common case, silently degrading trust in the automation.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The scheduled usage-schedule-check job persists a watermark of the last reported week and month, and on the next run after a missed boundary, catches up and sends the missed report instead of silently no-op-ing.
- [ ] Add a test simulating a machine asleep over a Sunday night boundary, waking Monday morning, that currently fails without the fix and passes with it.

title: tg-ctl: malformed rig usage --json can crash the /spend report formatter
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
composeUsageReport in tg-ctl only validates that parsed.periods is an object; formatUsagePeriod then dereferences p.totals and Object.entries(p.by_model) unconditionally. A syntactically valid but differently-shaped JSON response (e.g. a future rig-cli change) throws a TypeError instead of hitting the existing could-not-parse fallback.

## User impact
The daemon persists the Telegram update offset before running the action handler, so a thrown exception here means the user's /spend command is silently dropped with no reply at all, and the same crash would also break the scheduled weekly/monthly push (see [PR #292](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/292)).

## Cost of inaction
Any drift in rig-cli's usage.py output shape silently breaks both the on-demand and scheduled usage report with no error surfaced to the user or in logs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every period, totals, and by_model field read from rig usage --json output is validated at runtime before formatting; an unexpected shape (null, wrong type, missing field) produces the existing friendly could-not-parse message instead of throwing.
- [ ] Add tests covering periods.week: null, a missing totals object, a missing by_model object, and a string where a number is expected, asserting no exception and a graceful error message in each case.

title: tg-ctl: long /daily report can exceed Telegram's message limit and be lost with no retry
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
composeDailyReport runs the stateful rig daily command, which advances its own watermark, before the daemon sends the unbounded result through a single raw sendMessage call instead of the existing 4096-character splitting transmitter.

## User impact
A backlog with enough merged pull requests to exceed Telegram's limit fails to send; since rig daily has already advanced its watermark, the next /daily reports nothing and the missed update is gone for good.

## Cost of inaction
Users relying on /daily as their what-shipped digest (added in [PR #292](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/292)) can silently miss an entire reporting period after a busy week.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The /daily report path splits or truncates output that exceeds Telegram's message-length limit before sending, using the existing splitting transmitter rather than a raw sendMessage call.
- [ ] rig daily's watermark only advances after a confirmed successful delivery, so a failed or truncated send can be retried on the next /daily instead of being permanently skipped.
- [ ] Add an integration test with an oversized report body and a simulated failed Bot API response, asserting the watermark did not advance and the report is not silently lost.

title: tg-ctl: /spend shows a misleading $0.00 for models rig usage marks unpriced

title: tg-ctl: scheduled usage HTML send does not escape report body content

title: tg: a file path mentioned in a rich HTML message is auto-attached, which silently downgrades the send to the basic tier and fails with a misleading 'only those HTML tags are supported' error
body:
## What
Reproduced on 2026-09-05 while sending a --tag decision message with --format html: a 'Where to look' bullet containing a repo-relative path to the ship script with a line number (the ship.sh file under the ci directory of agent-tools, line 2708) matched the auto-attach rule (existing file paths in text are attached as documents). Because a message with an attachment is sent as a caption (basic tier), every rich tag (h3, table, ul, hr) became invalid, and tg failed with the basic-tier tag list and 'Escape raw <, >, and &' — nothing about the attachment. --dry-run reports 'does not support attachments (1 document)' only under --tag report, while under --tag decision it shows the tag error. The escalation format REQUIRES a file:line 'where to look' section, so every properly formatted decision that names a path that happens to exist relative to the cwd hits this. Fix: never auto-attach from a rich-tier (or escalation-tagged) message; when a message has both rich tags and an attachment, send the attachment separately or say so in the error; make the error name the attached path.

## Why (motivation)
The escalation gate demands file references and the auto-attach rule punishes exactly that; agents burn several attempts and Alex gets fewer, later escalations.

## User impact
Alex receives decision requests on the first try in the readable table format instead of agents giving up or sending free text after three failed attempts.

## Cost of inaction
Every escalation that names a real file keeps failing with a wrong error, and agents keep inventing workarounds around the format gate.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A --tag decision message whose 'Where to look' names an existing file path sends as a Rich Message without attaching the file; a test covers it.
- [ ] When auto-attach would force the basic tier, the error names the offending path and the auto-attach rule instead of the tag list.
- [ ] --dry-run reports the auto-attached path under every tag, not only report.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body: Second finding from the same incident (2026-09-05): after removing the auto-attached path the real send still failed, and the last output line was again the basic-tier tag list. The actual refusal was printed ABOVE it: "Refusing: --title contains a ticket reference (HYP-1440) — move it into the message body." Two more defects to fix here: (1) --dry-run does not validate --title at all, so a title that the real send refuses passes the dry-run (it reported OK); (2) every refusal ends with the generic 'Only those HTML tags are supported. Escape raw <, >, and &' block, so a caller reading the last line (or a tail -n 2) sees the wrong reason. The generic tag-list footer should only be printed for an actual tag violation, and --dry-run must run the same title checks as the real send.

title: tg: drop the question tag — only the standard tags stay (answer, decision, problem, report); a question is a decision request
body:
## What
Alex (2026-09-05): agents must use only the standard message tags, and there is no separate question type: an open question for him IS a decision request and must be sent as --tag decision in the decision-request format. Today tg still accepts --tag question (header QUESTION with an orange marker), the decision-request-format hook treats decision, problem and question as three escalation tags, and the decision-request-discipline skill tells agents to use tg --tag decision or --tag question. Two names for the same escalation split the format rules and let agents pick the softer one; Alex wants one typed vocabulary.

Alex sees every open question from an agent as a proper decision request with options, pros and cons, and a recommendation, never as a loosely typed question he has to interpret.

Agents keep sending question-tagged messages that look like a home-made format, and the escalation gate keeps two code paths to maintain.

title: tg: refuse to send a message containing a banned word from the shared dictionary (DICT.json next to the global CLAUDE.md), printing the replacement
body:
## What
Alex (2026-09-05): agents keep writing banned words (the invented verb for 'fixed' spelled with the stem почт-, 'скамейка' for bench, 'сел/лёг' for applied, 'land/landing' in Russian text, 'форк' to Alex, flattery phrases) despite the bans in his global CLAUDE.md, because prose rules are not enforced. He now keeps a machine-readable dictionary at ~/.claude/DICT.json (created today: version 1, a list of rules with id, regex pattern, flags, optional only_if_cyrillic, replacement, why). tg must load it (path override via TG_DICT_PATH, default ~/.claude/DICT.json; a missing file is not an error, a malformed file is a loud warning and no gate) and check the title, body and caption of EVERY outgoing message (all tags, all formats, files' captions too) against every rule; on a match refuse to send, exit non-zero, and print each hit with the rule id, the matched text with a little context, and the suggested replacement. --dry-run runs the same check. No self-service bypass flag: the agent rewrites the message. The check must ignore text inside <code> and <pre> blocks (quoting a banned word to discuss it is legitimate) and must strip HTML tags before matching so a tag boundary cannot hide a word. Document the file format in tg help format and in the installed tg skill; add tests with the real DICT.json shape (stem-based rules such as the почт- one must catch forms not listed anywhere).

Three rounds of prose bans failed; only a gate at the sending tool stops the words from reaching Alex.

## User impact
Alex stops reading reports with made-up words he has banned three times; an agent that slips gets told the exact word and the replacement and resends in one step.

title: tg-ctl ask: honour --timeout beyond the 115s hook cap, auto-deliver a queued decision to a re-run of the same deterministic request, and tell the truth about why the asker went away
body:
## What
Incident 2026-09-04 20:27 (Alex, terminal, 2026-09-05): gh ship on stt-cli PR 32 raised the external-review hatch; the hatch helper called tg-ctl ask with --timeout 900, but tg-ctl ignores the flag and caps EVERY ask at ASK_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 115 s (a budget meant for Claude Code's 120 s hook window). At 20:29:05 the ask gave up, the hatch recorded 'denied: no reply', ship refused, the PR is still open. Alex tapped Approve 53 minutes later and got: queued Approve for stt — this daemon can't prove a later reconnect is the SAME request, so it won't auto-deliver; tap again. That text is wrong on two counts: the asker is dead (it timed out, nothing will reconnect), and the request id IS content-derived and stable (the hatch request id is a hash of gate, PR and commit), so a re-run of gh ship 32 would present the very same id and the queued approval could be applied to it without any promptTurnId. Three changes: (1) tg-ctl ask parses --timeout and uses it as the total budget (cap 24 h; the 115 s default stays only when no --timeout is given, i.e. for Claude Code hook callers); (2) the ask client sends a final farewell line before closing on its own timeout so the daemon can distinguish asker-timed-out from dropped (daemon restart or killed), and every abandoned or queued card text states the real reason (the asking process gave up after 115 s) instead of 'can't prove'; (3) a queued decision on a request whose id is deterministic (no promptTurnId, id supplied by the caller) is delivered immediately to the next ask that arrives with the same requestId within a retention window (default 24 h), with a Telegram edit saying the earlier Approve was applied to the re-run, and the card tells Alex the exact command to re-run (the original question carries the gate, PR and repo). Related: [tg-cli#267](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/267), [tg-cli#100](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/100), [tg-cli#235](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/235), [tg-cli#149](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/149), [agent-tools#214](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/214).

## Why (motivation)
The 115 s cap silently overrides every caller's timeout, so every hatch approval that takes Alex longer than two minutes is lost, and the daemon then blames a missing proof it never needed.

## User impact
Alex taps Approve on his phone once, whenever he gets to it, and the agent's next ship attempt goes through; he stops being told to tap again for a request that nothing is waiting on.

## Cost of inaction
Every hatch approval slower than two minutes keeps dying, PRs stay unmerged, and Alex keeps re-tapping cards that lead nowhere.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tg-ctl ask --timeout 900 keeps the Telegram card live for 900 s (test with a fake daemon clock); without --timeout the budget stays 115 s.
- [ ] When the ask client times out it tells the daemon so; the card then says the asking process gave up after N seconds and what to re-run, never 'can't prove a later reconnect is the same request'.
- [ ] A tap on such a card is stored; a new ask with the same deterministic requestId within 24 h receives that decision immediately, and the card is edited to say it was applied; covered by a test with the real hatch request id shape.
- [ ] Docs (README, tg-ctl --help) describe the three behaviours.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: Empirical study of Claude Code prompts inside tmux: how to tell whether a permission or question is still pending, and wire the findings into tg-ctl
body:
## What
Alex has asked several times (again on 2026-09-05: how can the daemon not know whether a question is still pending? how many times have I asked to properly research Claude Code and how to work with it in tmux) for a real investigation instead of guesses. Deliverable: a reproducible study, run against a REAL Claude Code in an isolated HOME inside a private tmux server, that answers with evidence: (a) what a PermissionRequest or AskUserQuestion prompt looks like in capture-pane for every prompt shape (Bash, Edit or Write, plan approval, AskUserQuestion with options, multi-question), including the exact deny label; (b) the hook lifecycle: what the PermissionRequest hook receives (fields, prompt id, turn id), what happens when the hook exceeds its timeout (does the terminal prompt appear, is a late hook reply honoured or ignored, does the prompt survive), and whether a second hook invocation for the same prompt ever happens; (c) whether a pending prompt is visible in the session transcript JSONL (last record types) or in any file or socket Claude Code exposes, so the daemon can check pending-ness WITHOUT screen scraping; (d) how a keypress injected via tmux send-keys is handled (digit only vs digit plus Enter, focus, alternate screen); (e) the same for opencode and codex where they show prompts. Write it up as a dated document under the repo docs directory (cc-tmux-prompts) in tg-cli with the scripts under the repo tools directory so it can be re-run when Claude Code updates, then implement in tg-ctl a single is-prompt-pending(paneId, requestId) predicate built on the strongest signal found, used by late delivery and by the abandoned-card texts (the card must say pending, answered in terminal, or asker gone, from evidence). Related: [tg-cli#267](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/267), [tg-cli#268](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/268), [tg-cli#100](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/100), [tg-cli#235](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/235).

## Why (motivation)
Every late-delivery and reconnect bug in tg-ctl comes from not knowing how Claude Code actually behaves; the fixes keep being written from assumptions and keep failing on Alex.

## User impact
Alex taps a card on his phone and either the agent gets the answer or the card says plainly that the prompt is already gone; no more guessing texts and no more tapping twice.

## Cost of inaction
The next Claude Code update breaks the injection heuristics again and nobody can tell what changed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The study document exists with dated findings, the Claude Code version tested, and one re-runnable script per finding; every claim cites its capture or log.
- [ ] tg-ctl exposes and uses an is-prompt-pending check based on the study; the abandoned and queued card texts derive their wording from it (pending, already answered in terminal, asker gone).
- [ ] Late delivery covers every prompt shape the study found, or the unsupported shapes are listed explicitly in the document.

title: tg-ctl: agents running outside tmux are invisible — show them as unreachable with the reason, and deliver to them through the Stop-hook inbox
body:
## What
Incident 2026-09-05 (Alex): Telegram could not reach the agents 'landing' and 'rig-fable'; tg-ctl status listed neither. Root cause: both were started by claude-rotate from plain Hyper terminal tabs (no TMUX in the environment), and tg-ctl discovers agents only via tmux list-panes and delivers only via tmux send-keys, so an agent outside tmux does not exist for it — silently. Two changes in tg-ctl: (1) discovery also scans the process table for interactive harness processes (claude, codex or opencode with a tty, not --print) that have no tmux pane, and status plus the target picker list them as 'unreachable: not in tmux (tty, cwd, --name)' with a hint how to move them into tmux, instead of omitting them; a message routed to such an agent gets an explicit reply, never a silent drop. (2) A fallback delivery channel that needs no tty: an inbox file per agent (keyed by session id or cwd plus name, under the tg-cli config dir); the already-installed Claude Code Stop hook (cc_hook_bridge Stop, agent-tools) checks the inbox at the end of every turn and, when a message is pending, returns the block decision with the message text as the reason, which Claude Code feeds back to the agent as its next instruction; the daemon marks it delivered and reacts on the Telegram message as today. Limits stated honestly in the docs: an idle agent (already stopped) receives the inbox message only at its next turn, so status must say 'delivery deferred until the agent is active'. Companion change in agent-tools (the Stop hook descriptor) and in claude-rotate (warn when started without TMUX, or wrap into a tmux window with --tmux) are separate tickets linked here.

## Why (motivation)
Silently not seeing an agent is the worst failure mode of the bridge; Alex could not tell whether the daemon was broken or the agent was gone.

## User impact
Alex, writing from his phone, either reaches every running agent or is told exactly why one is unreachable and how to fix it, instead of messages vanishing.

## Cost of inaction
Every agent started outside tmux keeps being unreachable from Telegram with no explanation.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] tg-ctl status and the target picker list every interactive claude, codex or opencode process that has no tmux pane as unreachable with tty, cwd and name; sending to it returns a clear reply, never a silent drop; tests with a fake process table. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-306-c1.md)

title: Codex loads hook config from both hooks.json and config.toml — tg-ctl's usage telemetry and rig's hook bridge need one shared representation
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex hit this directly in a real codex session today, alongside several other codex startup warnings. title: Permission pane-inject: truncated-identity prefix match and TOCTOU can approve the wrong command
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Three independent review-cli reviewers (Opus/correctness, Codex/consistency, Fable/architect — surfaced while sweeping/merging [PR #266](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/266), tg-cli#263) independently found the same class of bug in [features/tg-ctl/permission-menu.ts](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/blob/main/features/tg-ctl/permission-menu.ts) and tg-ctl's pane-inject success path: (1) the truncated-identity fallback in permissionMenuMatchesRequest matches on a plain prefix+word-boundary regex built from a 100-char hook-normalize truncation that usually does NOT land on a word boundary, so for the long commands this feature targets the match is either dead (safe direction, but useless) or, per Fable's trace, can match a materially different command sharing the same prefix past char 100 — the exact wrong-command-approval the line-exact match elsewhere in this file was hardened to prevent; (2) Codex separately traced a capture/inject race where a stale permission A resolves locally, a new permission B appears in the same pane position before send-keys fires, and the post-injection check reports A delivered because it only checks 'is SOME menu still live', not 'is the ORIGINAL menu still live'; (3) Opus found the pane-delivered success path writes into answeredButtons, the cache the reconnect-deliver code deliberately avoids touching for permissions specifically to prevent replaying a stale decision to a later re-fire of the same requestId. All three are already live on main (confirmed via git diff against the PR's merge base — none of this is introduced by tg-cli#263's own harness-event-agent-label fix or by the sweep's merge), so tg-cli#263 was shipped on its own separate, unrelated fix without being blocked on this.

## User impact
A tapped Approve/Reject on a permission prompt can silently apply to a DIFFERENT command than the one the human saw and approved, for any command near or over the ~100-char hook-normalize truncation cap (the exact class of command — long, dangerous, near a timeout — this pane-inject feature was built to handle).

## Cost of inaction
The approval-scope-confusion bug ships silently to every user of tg-ctl's pane-inject permission flow; the next incident report ('I approved X but Y ran') will cost far more to diagnose after the fact than fixing the boundary/race check now.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] permissionMenuMatchesRequest's truncated-identity branch either requires the boundary that makes it safe or is removed in favor of always queuing on a truncated identity
- [ ] the post-injection recapture in tg-ctl distinguishes 'the same permission resolved' from 'a different permission now occupies the same menu position' before reporting delivered, with a regression test covering a menu swap between capture and send-keys
